Cryptography in Faraday: specifications, code and checks

Every cryptographic action in Faraday, 110 in all. The index, the actions and the list of libraries below are generated from Faraday's manifest, docs/crypto/actions.toml, at release 0.2.0 (SHA-256 e175b3ab42660df464731639eb087edbc5a6c0fe9d5103890dd3fffe0ae5254c), and none of them is written by hand. Faraday's own checks hold the manifest to the code: a cryptographic function the manifest does not cover, a change to one since its entry was last reviewed, or a change to the cryptographic code since the last passing cross-check fails Faraday's checks. The page is generated again each time the website is published for a new release.

Faraday's approach

Faraday follows published specifications: BIPs, SLIPs, RFCs and conventions other wallets already use. Where a specification has an established implementation, Faraday uses it as a library instead of writing its own. A library is code others wrote, published as a Rust crate and pinned to one version; Faraday's own code calls it, checks what goes in and comes out, refuses what it cannot verify, and does every step the library does not. Faraday writes code of its own only where no established implementation exists or none fits its rules for keys, and says why. Where no specification exists, Faraday writes its own, labelled "Own specification, not yet reviewed outside Faraday" until someone outside reviews it. Each action is checked against its specification's published test vectors where there are any, and its results are compared with a second implementation: code others wrote where it exists, otherwise a second version Faraday's authors wrote, which is not an outside check. Actions with no second implementation are marked not cross-checked.

Each row below is one action. Specification is what it follows. Code is the libraries it uses and the crate of Faraday's code that calls them. Cross-checked with is what its results are compared with. The full rule is on the Standards page.

  • Faraday's second version44Compared with a second implementation Faraday's authors wrote, in Python; not checked against an outside source.
  • Not cross-checked26Compared with no second implementation.

Action

Reads seed words typed, pasted or scanned, and checks their count and checksum.

Specification

BIP 39, Mnemonic code for generating deterministic keys, Deployed

Code

Library: unicode-normalization 0.1.25, by the unicode-rs developers.

Library: sha2 0.11.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Faraday's code: core/faraday-bip: The sentence is read in NFKD and split on Unicode whitespace; the first word not in the list is reported by position; a word typed by pinyin, zhuyin, kana or hangul is composed to the listed word.

Written by Faraday

BIP-39 entry and display: words typed by pinyin, zhuyin, kana or hangul, the last word's candidates, the explorer's view of the checksum (faraday-bip::bip39) · Faraday's own specification

How a person types and sees the words is Faraday's own.

Decision F178

BIP-39 mnemonics: entropy to words and back, the checksum, a word's place in its list (faraday-bip::bip39) · One exists but does not fit Faraday's rules for keys

The Rust BIP-39 library's word lookup takes a time that follows the secret words; Faraday's looks each word up in constant time and is tested against that library and the reference.

Does not fit: bip39 2.2.2 finds a word by a binary search or a scan that stops at it (find_word) and packs entropy with a branch on each bit (from_entropy_in), so the time it takes follows the secret words

Decision F180

Cross-check

Compared with others' code: python-mnemonic, by Trezor (SatoshiLabs), and bip39_slip39, by the btclib developers (a second reader: wordlists, entropy, indices, checksums and the seed in the ten languages).

Area bip39

Faraday's code faraday_bip::bip39

Compared with python-mnemonic (bip39/); bip39_slip39 (bip39-slip39/) answering every operation beside it.

Checked first: Its vendored files are hashed against references.sha256 before any run, and a published vector's answer is required of the reference as well as of Faraday; python-mnemonic's own to_hd_master_key is checked against the seed's master key, as a second BIP-32 master; its wheel is hashed too, and a published vector's answer is required of bip39_slip39 as well.

Vectors The ten wordlists; every vector of tools/vectors/bip39/vectors.json in Faraday's languages; the Japanese vectors with non-ASCII passphrases.

Random cases Entropy to words and back in every language and length; seeds under random ASCII passphrases; a changed word, an unknown word, a word too many or too few; every valid last word.

Differences Both read a BIP-39 sentence in NFKD, so composed words and the Japanese vectors as published parse on both sides (owner, 2026-10-23).

A passphrase typed in Faraday is printable ASCII, at most 256 bytes; python-mnemonic takes any text. Faraday's vector tests and start-up self-test give a non-ASCII passphrase as its NFKD bytes, and the area checks that a typed one, or one past 256 bytes, is still refused.

When it runs Before every release, with a new seed and about ten times the cases.

Last passing run Seed 5be11ec606a76d2767f225b8992c45fe · 30000 cases

github.com/bitcoinpasada/faraday

Secret handling

none: no secret leaves faraday-keys

A word is found by comparing it with every entry of its list in constant time (subtle), and the entropy's bits are written without a branch; the sentence is gathered by a masked scan, and its length follows the words, as BIP-39 requires; the code states no other timing.

The word buffer and the indices are Secret values, zeroized when dropped; the Mnemonic wipes its indices when dropped.

Limits

Word counts of 12, 15, 18, 21 and 24 only.

A word not in the chosen list is refused and its position reported.

A checksum that fails is refused.

Faraday's own calls

Word entry by readings and kana: typed readings find the listed words. Neutral.

github.com/bitcoinpasada/faraday

Secret handling

none: no secret leaves faraday-keys

A word is found by comparing it with every entry of its list in constant time (subtle), and the entropy's bits are written without a branch; the sentence is gathered by a masked scan, and its length follows the words, as BIP-39 requires; the code states no other timing.

The sentence, the salt and the seed are Secret values, zeroized when dropped; the key holds its words and passphrase in zeroizing buffers until it is removed.

Limits

A passphrase longer than 256 bytes, or with a byte outside 0x20 to 0x7E, is refused.

Nothing is added while a stick is attached.

Faraday's own calls

A passphrase is printable ASCII, at most 256 bytes. BIP 39 allows any NFKD text, so a wallet made elsewhere with another passphrase cannot be restored here; a letter outside the range typed into a passphrase field is refused. Conservative, F155.

Action

Makes a master key and its fingerprint from a seed or an extended private key, by BIP 32.

Specification

BIP 32, Hierarchical Deterministic Wallets, Deployed

Code

Library: bitcoin 0.32.102, by the rust-bitcoin developers.

Library: secp256k1 0.29.1, by the rust-bitcoin developers (rust-secp256k1), over libsecp256k1, by Bitcoin Core's libsecp256k1 project (bitcoin-core/secp256k1).

Library: hmac 0.13.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Library: sha2 0.11.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Library: base16ct 1.0.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Faraday's code: core/faraday-bip: An extended private key typed or scanned is decoded by Faraday's own strict rules (78 bytes, version, zero parent and child number at depth 0, zero pad byte, scalar in 1..n) before bitcoin sees it; the key is kept on a pinned page; the fingerprint and a 32-byte identity (SHA-256 of the public key and chain code) are worked out once.

fuzz xkey

Cross-check

Compared with others' code: btclib-wallet's bip32, by the btclib developers, on btclib's own curve; and hdkeychain from btcd v0.27.0, by the btcd developers, on decred's secp256k1.

Compared, for one part, with Faraday's second version, written by Faraday's authors in Python; that part is not checked against an outside source: the three rules of a strict reader that hdkeychain does not make: which versions it takes (BIP-32's xprv and tprv, xpub and tpub, from btclib's network table; btclib reads SLIP-132's too and hdkeychain any version), a version of the other kind than the key's data, and a depth-0 key with a parent fingerprint or an index, in area_bip32.py and bip32_ref.py.

Area bip32

Faraday's code faraday_bip::keys (master, private derivation), faraday_bip::xkey (strict decoding), bitcoin's Xpub::derive_pub

Compared with btclib-wallet's bip32 over btclib and ecc (btclib/), on btclib's own curve with libsecp256k1 turned off, through bip32_ref.py, and hdkeychain from btcd v0.27.0 (btcd/, Go, decred's secp256k1); the versions a strict reader takes (BIP-32's four, from btclib's network table), a version whose kind differs from the key's data, and a depth-0 key with a parent or an index are ours.

Checked first: The wheels and the vendored Go tree are hashed against references.sha256 before any run; check_driver runs btclib against BIP-32's vectors 1 to 5 and the invalid keys of vector 5 before anything else, and every vector is asked of hdkeychain too.

Vectors BIP-32's vectors 1 to 5 (tools/vectors/bip32/), python-mnemonic's master keys.

Random cases Seeds of 16 to 64 bytes on every network, random paths with every index, public derivation against private, keys broken one rule at a time and the master-key import, each judged by btclib and by hdkeychain.

Differences Hdkeychain reads a key of any version, a key whose version is a private one over a public key's data (or the reverse), and a depth-0 key with a parent fingerprint or an index. Faraday refuses all three, as btclib refuses the last; where one applies and btclib refuses, hdkeychain is not asked (uncovered in area_bip32.py), so Faraday's strict reader is not retired.

When it runs Before every release, with a new seed and about ten times the cases.

Action

Holds a key in memory blinded and on pinned pages.

Specification

Own specification (no decision)

github.com/bitcoinpasada/faraday

Secret handling

none: no secret leaves faraday-keys

Secret and Pinned comparison is constant time (subtle's ConstantTimeEq, documented in secret.rs and pinned.rs).

A Secret and a Pinned page are zeroized on drop. Not reached: a secret while it is live in a plain type, the stack and registers, memory other code allocates, a copy in freed heap until the process ends (the next lock on the device), and anything outside the process (none on the device; the computer's own on the desktop).

Limits

Pinning is a feature of the desktop app and of the stick and Pi images (faraday-crypto's pin-pages); a build without it holds the same value unpinned.

Faraday's own calls

A key's signing context is blinded from the session's randomness. Neutral.

Area codex32

Faraday's code faraday_bip::codex32

Compared with python-codex32 (codex32/); rust-codex32 at a pinned commit (rust-codex32/), a program outside the workspace: parsing, checksums, the threshold and a threshold of 0's share index, interpolate_at for a fresh set's shares; volvelle-website's checksum worksheet run as a program over every worksheet of 48 and 74 characters; the worksheet of 127 characters written in the area from python-codex32's polymod.

Checked first: Its vendored files are hashed against references.sha256 before any run (the Rust programs' sources included, built offline by run.sh with the toolchain on the PATH), and a published vector's answer is required of the reference as well as of Faraday; rust-codex32 and python-codex32 must give the same answer where both are asked; two rules BIP 93 states that neither enforces (the master seed's sizes, the order shares are handed out) are written in the area from the BIP's text, and the worksheet of 127 characters from BIP 93's polymod alone.

Vectors Every vector of tools/vectors/bip93/, the 55 invalid strings included; volvelle-website's worksheet cells (tools/vectors/codex32-volvelle/); the booklet's checksum, derivation, recovery, addition, translation and fusion tables (tools/vectors/codex32-booklet/); the Codex32QR profile's sets (tools/vectors/codex32qr/).

Random cases secrets, splits (the same randomness), recovery, derived shares, corrupted strings; fresh sets of every threshold up to 31 strings at 48, 74 and 127 characters, the checksum worksheets of their strings and of corrupted ones, checksums made on a sheet, translation and recovery symbols, translation worksheets.

Differences Codex32: Faraday recovers only from exactly k shares without the secret, and derives a share only from exactly k strings at an unused index; the reference also takes more strings or a used index.

The codex32 seed sizes, which the references leave to their caller, are written in the area from the BIP's own sentence. Volvelle's sheet works the checksum itself, so a string of 48 or 74 characters whose checksum is not the one the sheet works is judged by that alone (holds false), not by its rows.

Convert a key's master seed

SpecificationBIP 32 · BIP 39 · SLIP-0039 · 3 morePublishedCodeLibrary: base16ct 1.0 (through core/faraday-crypto)Faraday's code: faraday/faraday-keysCross-checked withNot cross-checked
Action

Writes a key's master seed as hex, its master extended private key, a SLIP-39 1 of 1, a SLIP-39 set of k of n or of groups, or a codex32 set, a key's words as Seed XOR parts, and a key's words as words, SeedQR, CompactSeedQR, hex entropy, word numbers or 4-letter starts, each read back through its standard's decoder to the key's wallet.

Specification

BIP 32, Hierarchical Deterministic Wallets, Deployed

BIP 39, Mnemonic code for generating deterministic keys, Deployed

SLIP-0039, Shamir's Secret-Sharing for Mnemonic Codes, Status not checked, vendored

BIP 93, codex32: Checksummed SSS-able BIP32 Seeds, Draft, vendored

SeedQR, SeedQR and CompactSeedQR, Convention, vendored

Seed XOR, Seed XOR, Coldcard's split of a seed into parts, Convention, vendored

Code

Library: base16ct 1.0.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Faraday's code: faraday/faraday-keys: Each conversion is given only for Reveal::PaperForm, and only when its result, read back through the standard's own decoder (hex, the strict xprv importer, SLIP-39's share, every share of a set parsed before any recovery and then a first and a last qualifying subset each recovered, codex32's parse of every share and recover from the first k and the last k), gives the key's master fingerprint; otherwise nothing is returned. A key's words written in another form are read back to the same entropy on the same list, so the same words and the same fingerprint, with no PBKDF2 run; SeedQR forms take English 12 or 24 words, and 4-letter starts English. A key with words is refused for SLIP-39 and codex32; SLIP-39 holds 16 and 32 bytes only; Seed XOR is given for a key on the English list only, the list its parts are restored on. A codex32 set of k above 0 takes its identifier from the randomness passed in, never the one of the key's fingerprint nor of its own set, so two sets of one key are not one set; the secret alone keeps the fingerprint's. A SLIP-39 set is made with an empty passphrase, the extendable flag set and iteration exponent 1, its identifier and shares from the randomness passed in, and a shape the split refuses is refused.

Checked against

tools/vectors/bip39

Published, by Trezor (SatoshiLabs), python-mnemonic's vectors; bip32JP's Japanese vectors.

Convert a typed SLIP-39 set

SpecificationSLIP-0039PublishedCodeLibrary: subtle 2.6Faraday's code: faraday/faraday-keysCross-checked withpython-shamir-mnemonicOthers' codeFaraday's second version
Action

Holds the SLIP-39 shares a person types, and from them writes a share at a member index (adding a share or replacing a lost one) or a new set of the same encrypted master secret, each read back before it is returned.

Specification

SLIP-0039, Shamir's Secret-Sharing for Mnemonic Codes, Status not checked, vendored

Code

Library: subtle 2.6.1, by the dalek-cryptography developers.

Faraday's code: faraday/faraday-keys: The typed shares are held as a transient value, never a key, and each is checked against the others as it is typed (one set; no member typed twice; no more members than the group's threshold). A share at a member index is derived from one group's quorum and read back by swapping it in for one of the quorum, which must give back, word for word, the share displaced; where the whole set is typed the swapped set must also recover the same EMS and parameters. A new set is split from the EMS recovered from the whole set's quorum: with the extendable flag set it takes a new identifier and the old one is refused, with it clear the identifier stays; every share is parsed and every member of every group takes part in a qualifying subset that must recover the same EMS and parameters. No passphrase is taken and nothing is decrypted.

Compared, for one part, with Faraday's second version, written by Faraday's authors in Python; that part is not checked against an outside source: slip39::check_gathered, Faraday's own rule on the shares typed (one set, no member twice, no more members than the threshold), which no judge in tools/crosscheck runs, and the held set and the read-back, which are tested here against the published vectors.

Area slip39

Faraday's code faraday_bip::slip39

Compared with python-shamir-mnemonic (slip39/), its recover_ems, split_ems and _interpolate for a set's EMS, a new split of it and a member at an index; bip39_slip39 (bip39-slip39/) answering each SLIP-39 operation beside it (not the two codex32 operations); python-codex32 (codex32/) for the codex32 side of the conversions and btclib (bip32_ref.py) for the fingerprint; the refusals of a member at an index before the arithmetic are ours (derive_refused), and so are the lengths the fixed 1 of 1 refuses, which no second judge covers.

Checked first: Its vendored files are hashed against references.sha256 before any run, and a published vector's answer is required of the reference as well as of Faraday, and of bip39_slip39 too; all 45 of its own vectors are run.

Vectors All 45 of tools/vectors/slip39/, each again through its EMS and its decryption.

Random cases Splits fed the same random bytes, which must match word for word; recovery from qualifying and short subsets and a changed word; the passphrase cipher; a set's EMS from a quorum, refused from a short or changed set, split again on the same random bytes (some under a new identifier where extendable) and a member added or a lost one made again at an index, each recovering the first set's secret, and a member refused at an index given, past 15, from a short quorum and across two groups; random seeds of 16 and 32 bytes through the fixed 1 of 1 against both libraries under the fingerprint's first 15 bits, recovered through both, and the lengths it refuses, against Faraday's own rule; the seed written as codex32 by Faraday and read by python-codex32, and a SLIP-39 set with a passphrase recovered by Faraday and by python-shamir-mnemonic, written as codex32 by Faraday and by python-codex32, the second read by Faraday, the same bytes both ways, the identifier's 20 bits written and the fingerprint (btclib's) compared on both sides.

Differences SLIP-39: Faraday refuses a group threshold of 1 over several groups; python-shamir-mnemonic makes the shares. The area checks that this still holds, so a change either way is seen.

Specification

Own specification (F171)

Code

Library: secp256k1 0.29.1, by the rust-bitcoin developers (rust-secp256k1), over libsecp256k1, by Bitcoin Core's libsecp256k1 project (bitcoin-core/secp256k1).

Library: bitcoin 0.32.102, by the rust-bitcoin developers.

Faraday's code: core/faraday-bip: Reads base58check with the bitcoin crate and holds Bitcoin Core's DecodeSecret rules itself: a version of 0x80 or 0xef, 32 bytes of key then nothing or exactly 0x01, a scalar in 1..n; the key is held on a pinned page in a signing context blinded from the key and, in faraday-keys, again from the session's randomness. Cross-check

Compared with others' code: Bitcoin Core v31.1, by the Bitcoin Core developers, which signs from descriptors of the same WIF what Faraday reads from it and shares libsecp256k1's curve maths with Faraday's; btclib, by the btclib developers, which decodes the WIF and works out its public key on its own curve.

Area sign

Faraday's code faraday_psbt::sign (every held key selected, deterministic Schnorr, both RFC 6979 nonce rules) and faraday_psbt::finalize

Compared with Bitcoin Core v31.1 on regtest (core_node.py): descriptorprocesspsbt signs from the held masters' keys, finalizepsbt finalizes and extracts, testmempoolaccept judges each finalized transaction over its funding on the node; BIP-340's reference (secp256k1lab) and Core's key.py for the deterministic nonces, over Core's script.py sighashes; python-ecdsa (the distribution's package) and btclib (btclib/, its own curve) as a second curve lineage, beside them: every ECDSA signature again under plain RFC 6979 or verified, every BIP-340 signature verified and made again; btclib-wallet's finalizer (psbt.finalize with its miniscript solver) finalizes every input Faraday finalizes again and gives the same scriptSig and witness; for each sweep, btclib reads the WIF (scalar, compression, public key) and signs and finalizes the sweep on its own curve, and python-ecdsa makes the first-nonce signature of each input again, byte for byte; python-bip380 (miniscript/) reads the leaves. Faraday's refusals and the inputs a wallet's rule leaves unsigned are ours, in area_sign.py.

Checked first: Core is the pinned release, hashed against its pin before every run; the vendored files are hashed against references.sha256; a published vector's answer is required of Core as well as of Faraday; every ECDSA and BIP-340 signature Core makes is checked to verify under the hash the area computes before that hash is used for Faraday's deterministic nonces.

Vectors BIP-174's signer, finalizer and extractor vectors; the Core-built spends of tools/vectors/psbt/ (2-of-3 sortedmulti, the Liana wallet down both paths, a taproot tree by a leaf and by the key path, BIP 387's taproot multisig), signed by every subset of their keys; the finalizer vectors there (or_b's smaller signature, the taproot leaves that tie by count, the taproot multisig and MuSig2 spends).

Random cases PSBTs of one to four inputs, each spending a funding output on the node: P2PKH, P2SH-P2WPKH, P2WPKH, multi/sortedmulti in P2SH, P2WSH and P2SH-P2WSH, P2TR key path, P2TR script path (pk, pkh, timelocked keys, or_d, multi_a) with the key path beside it, miniscript in P2WSH and P2SH-P2WSH; held and foreign keys, cosigners' signatures already on (Core's), every standard sighash type, timelocks met and not; Core's signatures (ECDSA byte for byte, BIP-340 by verification and the deterministic nonce), each final scriptSig and witness and the extracted transaction Core's, the cleared fields, and every finalized transaction accepted by Core's mempool; an origin that derives another key refused; sweeps: a WIF key's P2PKH, P2WPKH and P2SH-P2WPKH outputs (P2PKH alone for an uncompressed key) spent beside another key's, signed by Core from the WIF and by faraday_psbt::sweep::sign, byte for byte, finalized and accepted by the mempool.

Differences PSBT signing: Faraday refuses to sign a SegWit v0 input with no previous transaction in a transaction of more than one input; Core signs it, and BIP-174's own signer vector is such a PSBT. The refusal is ours, checked and counted. Faraday holds a finalized input to the same rule and refuses the PSBT when such an input is final, except a taproot one, whose final witness is the coordinator's.

PSBT signing, wallets: Faraday signs an input spent from a script of several keys (a multi of two or more, a miniscript naming two or more, a taproot script path whose carried leaves name two or more with its internal key, or are not its whole tree) only for a registered wallet that holds one of its keys and whose script it is; Core signs any. The area refuses, by a rule of its own, where no wallet the request registers holds a held key and gives the input, and counts it only where Faraday's refusal is that the wallet is not registered. A miniscript or a taproot tree of one key is signed only through such a wallet, and is otherwise left unsigned while the rest is signed (F141); the area takes Core's signatures off it. Half the corpus's multi, miniscript and taproot-tree inputs come with their wallet registered, so their signatures are still compared. A registered tree's every leaf has its wait met, since Faraday refuses a path that can never be valid, which the area does not work out.

PSBT signing: Faraday refuses a PSBT any input of which asks for a NONE or SINGLE sighash, and one that none of the held keys can sign: dangers no hold accepts (F136). Core signs the first and answers the second with nothing signed. The area expects both refusals by a rule of its own, counting a held key as taking part as Faraday's inspection does (a miniscript or a taproot tree only through a wallet in use), checks that Faraday's refusal names the danger, and counts them.

Taproot pkh leaves: Faraday signs a taproot leaf that checks its key by hash but does not finalize it: miniscript 12's finalizer looks the key up among the ECDSA origins and panics, and would push 33 bytes where the leaf hashed 32. Core finalizes such a leaf; the area takes the signatures under it off before Core finalizes, and counts each input Core would otherwise have finalized another way.

btclib's finalizer writes no taproot leaf that is neither a single key nor multi_a, and refuses to choose among leaves a PSBT signs: an input of another leaf is judged by Core alone (counted as a known difference), and btclib is given only the signatures of the leaf Faraday spent. It writes a plain multisig from the smallest m signatures on hand where Core and Faraday write the first m signers': btclib is given only the signatures Faraday's input carries, so it judges the script written from them and Core judges which were chosen.

When it runs Before every release, with a new seed and about ten times the cases.

Secret handling

none: no secret leaves faraday-keys

libsecp256k1 documents its key multiplication as constant time; the base58 decode is not stated to be.

The decoded buffer is zeroized before the reader returns, but base58ck's own scratch and result vectors are freed unwiped, until the next lock (ESTABLISHED §4.8); the key is held on a pinned page and erased when it is dropped, at Done, a lock or leaving the Sweep sheet.

Limits

A key is swept and never kept: no vault record, no key slot, no backup.

A WIF of the other network kind is refused.

Faraday's own calls

A WIF key is never loaded as a key or kept: it lives for one sweep. Conservative, F171.

Action

Code

Faraday's code: core/faraday-bip: The script is derived from the keys of the policy on a verification-only context; an index of 2^31 or more is refused; the search takes the receive and change address at each index in turn, nearest first. The witness bytes of a satisfaction (btclib assembles one and area sign compares Faraday's finalizer); a wallet with more than 64 ways to spend, for which Faraday states none; hash locks and locks in seconds, which the corpus does not generate; and a wallet btclib cannot read (none yet).

Random cases Wallets of the Liana, Nunchuk, Sparrow and recovery shapes in wsh() and sh(wsh()), multi/sortedmulti in sh(), wsh(), sh(wsh()), tr() with trees of one to six leaves or a lone sortedmulti_a, over random accounts on every network, at random indices of both chains; the same made not sane, refused; recovery wallets of both forms with one to three recovery paths, and the ways each wallet's coins move spent at their lock times.

Differences Miniscript: Faraday reads sortedmulti_a only as a tr()'s one leaf; BIP 387 allows it deeper in a tree, and Core reads it there. Two of Bitcoin Core's sane miniscripts are refused, as miniscript refuses them: or_b(0,a:0), which has no satisfaction, and a d: used as a unit under Tapscript. Each is checked and counted; btclib is not asked the deeper sortedmulti_a. btclib says nothing of "needs a signature" for a malleable miniscript (BIP 379 does not), so that property is compared where Core calls the miniscript non-malleable.

Action

Reads another wallet's export (Coldcard JSON and multisig configuration files, Specter DIY's addwallet command) as a wallet and checks the first address it states; writes a native SegWit single-key wallet as Coldcard's file for Wasabi, and any wallet but a MuSig2 or silent payments one as Specter DIY's addwallet command.

Specification

BIP 388, Wallet Policies for Descriptor Wallets, Complete

RFC 8259, The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format, Status not checked

Code

Library: bitcoin 0.32.102, by the rust-bitcoin developers.

Library: serde_json 1.0.151, by David Tolnay.

Library: base16ct 1.0.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Faraday's code: core/faraday-bip: JSON is read by serde_json, behind Faraday's refusal of a key named twice and of a nesting deeper than 32 (and of a text over 1 MiB); a Coldcard export's stated first address is derived and compared; a multisig file with more than fifteen cosigners is refused at the sixteenth. An account key alone becomes a wallet of the kind its path's purpose names (44 legacy, 49 nested SegWit, 84 native SegWit, 86 taproot), and a purpose of 45, 48 or 87 is a cosigner's key and no wallet on its own; a key of a test network is taken as testnet unless the session is already on a test network; the file for Wasabi is written only for a native SegWit single-key wallet whose key has an origin at exactly 84h/0h/0h or 84h/1h/0h. Specter DIY's addwallet command is read with its name before the last `&`, its descriptor's checksum checked where it has one (Specter DIY drops it unread), and keys none of which carries a derivation as the two chains; a single-key or multisig wallet is written without its keys' derivations and with no checksum, as Sparrow writes it, any other with them.

Written by Faraday

The JSON visitor that refuses a key named twice and counts depth (faraday-bip::json) · Only the part used is written

serde_json reads the text; Faraday refuses a key named twice and a nesting deeper than 32.

Decision F180

Random cases single-key wallets (P2PKH, P2SH-P2WPKH, P2WPKH, P2TR), sortedmulti in P2WSH, P2SH-P2WSH and P2SH of one to fifteen keys, a miniscript in P2WSH, a taproot tree and a taproot sortedmulti_a, on mainnet and testnet keys, each as a descriptor (multipath with and without checksum, receive and change lines, labelled, receive alone, Core's listdescriptors, Specter Desktop's file, Specter DIY's addwallet with and without its keys' derivations) or as the files that state its kind (Coldcard's export and multisig file, Caravan's, Electrum's, Cobo's, Wasabi's, a key alone, a BSMS descriptor record), in BIP-32's or SLIP-132's spelling; damaged by a wrong checksum, a wrong first address, a SLIP-132 version of another script or another paths line; key records signed by btclib in each header form, with or without damage, and Faraday's own record of random seeds.

Differences Still ours, expected from Faraday's rule: a SLIP-132 version that names another script than the file's (F155), a BSMS paths line other than /0/*,/1/* or No path restrictions, which Faraday reads as the two chains (F64), a BSMS descriptor that is not a template, a key record whose description is over eighty characters or whose token is not BIP 129's; and which account of a Coldcard export, which pair of a listdescriptors, and what each field of every format means, the area's reading of each format's documentation; a checksum in Specter DIY's addwallet, which Specter DIY drops unread and Faraday checks, is refused when Core's code calls it wrong; and the reading of each format's documentation.

A file whose stated first address is not its wallet's is refused.

Compared with others' code: Bitcoin Core v31.1 itself (getdescriptorinfo, deriveaddresses) and its functional-test framework, by Bitcoin Core's contributors; python-bip380, by Antoine Poinsot, for the miniscript's validity, sanity and script; btclib-wallet's descriptors and miniscript, by the btclib developers, on btclib's own curve, for the descriptor's kind, checksum, script at an index and the miniscript's script.

Compared, for one part, with Faraday's second version, written by Faraday's authors in Python; that part is not checked against an outside source: the lift of a miniscript to a boolean formula over its keys and waits, written in area_compile.py from the fragments' meanings (rust-miniscript's own lift is not used), and the rules by which a policy is refused (a threshold of 0 or above its parts, a lock of 0, a key twice, nothing typed), which no outside compiler states.

Area compile

Faraday's code faraday_bip::compile::compile (a concrete policy to a wsh() or tr() descriptor, the keys it names, the ways it can be spent and the script it pays at an index), over rust-miniscript's policy compiler

Compared with Bitcoin Core v31.1's bitcoind on regtest (getdescriptorinfo and deriveaddresses), with its descriptors.py (BIP-380's checksum); btclib-wallet's descriptors and miniscript (btclib/, on btclib's own curve) for the kind, checksum, script at an index and keys; Antoine Poinsot's python-bip380 (miniscript/) for the miniscript's validity, sanity and script, and its fragments for the lift to a formula, which is ours (lift, in area_compile.py).

Checked first: Its vendored files are hashed against references.sha256 before any run; Core's release tarball is checked against its pinned SHA-256 (tools/reference/core/release.pin) before every run, and the node's version is asked; the self-test makes Faraday's descriptor wrong and the lift wrong, and each is caught.

The script itself: no other compiler makes rust-miniscript's choice, so only that it is valid, sane and means the policy is judged; hash locks, locks in seconds and the time flag of older, which the corpus does not generate; a policy that names a key by a fingerprint token of a loaded key; policies of more than six keys.

Vectors none: no compiler states a script for a policy (rust-miniscript, sipa's and the Go and Python ones choose differently), so the answers are judged by what the descriptor is and means.

Random cases Policies of and, or (with weights), thresh, pk, after and older of one to six keys, each key written as an account key with its origin, compiled for wsh() and for tr() (a key beside the rest, which the compiler takes as the internal key), on mainnet and testnet keys, read at random indices of both chains; refusals: a threshold of 0 or above its parts, a lock of 0, a key twice, nothing typed.

Differences A single key as a tr() policy: rust-miniscript's compile_tr takes the key as the internal key, is left with no leaf and refuses it (Empty Miniscript compilation); Faraday refuses it too, in its own words, and the area counts the refusal. python-bip380 writes a v: over a multi_a, at any depth, as OP_NUMEQUAL OP_VERIFY where BIP 379 and Core write OP_NUMEQUALVERIFY, so such a leaf must equal btclib's script but for that (counted); the output key, which commits to the leaf, is Core's and btclib's. python-bip380 types and_b's e as f_X s_X f_Y s_Y where BIP 379 has e_X e_Y s_X s_Y, so it calls thresh(1,X,a:and_b(pk(A),s:pk(B))) malleable where BIP 379, Core and btclib call it sane. Its thresh leaves the first part out of e, s and m, so it never calls a thresh expressive and calls an or_c over one malleable, where the same three call it sane. Its 0 is not s where BIP 379's is, so l:X and u:X lose X's s. Such a miniscript is asked of python-bip380 again with those three rules as BIP 379's, must be sane then and is counted; any other reason python-bip380 gives stops the area. Its thresh of 1 never sets its lock fields, so reading one inside a thresh of 2 or more raises a TypeError, where BIP 379, Core and btclib read it. Such a miniscript is read again with those fields set from its parts, as Core keeps them, and is counted; any other error stops the area.

Action

Turns dice rolls into entropy by one of three published procedures, and cautions about runs, sequences and skew.

Specification

Dice hashing of Coldcard and SeedSigner, Coldcard rolls.py, SeedSigner, EntropyLab, Keystone and BitBox dice procedures, Convention

Code

Library: sha2 0.11.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Faraday's code: core/faraday-entropy: Hashed rolls are SHA-256 of the rolls as ASCII digits, truncated to the strength; the second procedure writes every 6 as 0 first; the third names every word from five rolls of 1 to 4 and a sixth read as a coin, and the checksum replaces the last word's low bits.

Written by Faraday

Dice, coin, card, hex and camera entropy accumulation and packing, and the mix of sources (faraday-entropy) · Faraday's own specification

An empty payload, which segno refuses.

Vectors SeedSigner's nine test SeedQRs (tools/vectors/seedqr/); every string and picture of the Codex32QR profile (tools/vectors/codex32qr/), each decoded by zbar and zxing-cpp.

Random cases Keys of every length and language, both codes and the words read back; digits and bytes malformed; payloads in each mode at each level and version limit; 48-character codex32 strings in either case as Codex32QR codes and the pictures written of them read back and decoded by zbar and zxing-cpp, other lengths refused; the pictures of a key's SeedQR and CompactSeedQR decoded by both and read by Faraday to the key's words; greyscale pictures and QR pictures of random size and scale read by Pillow and zlib.

Differences SeedQR digits: SeedSigner reads a string with 1 to 3 digits more than 48 or 96 (it drops the tail) and one with a sign or a space inside a group of four (int() takes them); Faraday refuses both (5 cases, each checked on both sides and counted). SeedSigner takes no CompactSeedQR of 20, 24 or 28 bytes either, and strips checksum bits for 12 and 24 words only; the corpus keeps Faraday's 15, 18 and 21 word compact form on the entropy itself.

Codex32QR: Faraday picks the mask Nayuki's encoder picks; the profile's encoder chose another for 6 of its 22 pictures. For those the area swaps the mask of Faraday's code for the picture's with qrcodegen.py's masking, requires the picture, and counts it.

Segno 1.6 writes a zero codeword where the pad codewords begin when the data, terminator included, ends on a codeword boundary with room left (its write_padding_bits adds 8 zero bits where none are due; ISO/IEC 18004 7.4.10 adds none): its code is Nayuki's with that codeword changed, which rqrr reads, counted as a known difference, the padding; Faraday's is the standard's.

Segno picks a mask by its own penalty rule, and for some payloads another than Nayuki's and Faraday's; the area requires that code to be Faraday's under the mask segno reports (Nayuki's masking swapped to it) and rqrr to read it, and counts each as a known difference, the mask choice, which a reader ignores.

The digit buffer is a fixed array inside a Secret and the module grid is zeroizing; both wipe on drop.

Limits

A SeedQR is made for any word count; one is read back only at 12 and 24 words: 48 or 96 digits, or 16 or 32 bytes.

The CompactSeedQR of 15, 18 or 21 words is the entropy itself, a form SeedSigner does not define.

The picture carries no wordlist language.

Faraday's own calls

The picture is a copy only when it is checked by a scan or typed words. Neutral, F29.

Checked first: Its vendored files are hashed against references.sha256 before any run, and a published vector's answer is required of the reference as well as of Faraday; SeedSigner's reader is looser than Faraday (it takes 49 digits, a sign inside a group, 20 to 28 bytes, and does not check the checksum of digits), so Faraday's own rule, the lengths and the digits, stands in front of it in area_seedqr.py and the checksum is embit's; SeedSigner runs in English for every language, the indices being the same; the profile's own pictures are read from their pixels and must be Faraday's code module for module; segno is asked for Faraday's version, level and mode and its mask forced, and its mask is read back from it, its padding quirk being modelled in Nayuki's code; rqrr reads Faraday's and segno's codes; the self-test makes each decoder's answer wrong (a payload's last byte changed) and must catch it.

An empty payload, which segno refuses.

SeedSigner takes no CompactSeedQR of 20, 24 or 28 bytes either, and strips checksum bits for 12 and 24 words only; the corpus keeps Faraday's 15, 18 and 21 word compact form on the entropy itself.

Codex32QR: Faraday picks the mask Nayuki's encoder picks; the profile's encoder chose another for 6 of its 22 pictures. For those the area swaps the mask of Faraday's code for the picture's with qrcodegen.py's masking, requires the picture, and counts it.

Segno 1.6 writes a zero codeword where the pad codewords begin when the data, terminator included, ends on a codeword boundary with room left (its write_padding_bits adds 8 zero bits where none are due; ISO/IEC 18004 7.4.10 adds none): its code is Nayuki's with that codeword changed, which rqrr reads, counted as a known difference, the padding; Faraday's is the standard's.

Segno picks a mask by its own penalty rule, and for some payloads another than Nayuki's and Faraday's; the area requires that code to be Faraday's under the mask segno reports (Nayuki's masking swapped to it) and rqrr to read it, and counts each as a known difference, the mask choice, which a reader ignores.

Secret handling

Reveal::BackupStick

GF(32) multiplication, the checksum's residue and the alphabet's lookup are written without a branch or a table index on a symbol's value, as the code documents; the code states no other timing.

The string, its payload and the seed are fixed arrays wiped on drop; a codex32 share record's string is a secret. A fresh set's share list is reserved at its full count before the first share is pushed, so no share is left in a block freed by a reallocation.

Limits

Seeds of 128, 160, 192, 224, 256 or 512 bits.

A threshold of 2 to 9, or 0 for the secret alone, and at most 31 strings.

A string that does not hold together, or whose checksum fails, is refused with the reason named.

A key of words is never split into codex32 strings.

Faraday's own calls

Recovery is from exactly k shares only. Conservative, F90.

The set's identifier is the first 20 bits of the master fingerprint, which puts 20 bits of it on every share. Neutral.

none: no secret leaves faraday-keys

Writes and reads a Krux encrypted code (KEF): a passphrase and a count of PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256 rounds over an id give an AES-256 key, and one of twelve versions (ECB, CBC, CTR or GCM, with or without compression) seals the bytes with the format's own check.

Specification

KEF, KEF, Krux's encrypted code, Convention

Code

Library: aes 0.9.3, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: cbc 0.2.1, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: ctr 0.10.1, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: aes-gcm 0.11.1, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: miniz_oxide 0.8.9 and 0.9.1, by the miniz_oxide developers, a port of Rich Geldreich's miniz.

Library: sha2 0.11.0, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: hmac 0.13.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Faraday's code: faraday/faraday-kef: Only the part used is written: the twelve versions of Krux's table, their padding and their checks, the tolerant reading of Krux's own inconsistencies, and the refusal of what Krux refuses to write (a hidden check ending in 0x00). A compressed code inflates under a limit. The PBKDF2 loop can stop and counts; it is one 32-byte block, checked against the library's PBKDF2 and RFC 7914's vectors.

Written by Faraday

KEF: the envelope, the version table, padding, the two SHA-256 checks and base43 (faraday-codec::kef, faraday-kef), and PBKDF2's loop over HMAC-SHA-256 for one block, with a cancel check (faraday-crypto::hash) · Only the part used is written

No library reads or writes this format. The pbkdf2 crate is one call that cannot stop, and a count of 100 million rounds must be stoppable.

Decision F219

Area kef

Faraday's code faraday_kef (seal, seal_with_key, open, open_with_key, suggest_versions), faraday_codec::kef::unwrap

Compared with krux's kef.py (krux/, unchanged), by the krux developers, on three small shims for the firmware's AES, SHA-256 and PBKDF2, and deflate modules (PyCA cryptography's AES, hashlib, zlib at wbits -10).

Checked first: The vendored files are hashed against references.sha256 before any run; krux's own vectors (tools/vectors/kef/) are required of the reference as well as of Faraday; every plaintext Faraday seals is opened by krux's decrypt, and every plaintext krux seals by Faraday, to the plaintext that went in.

The text forms and the classifier (krux's kef.py holds neither), the Reveal variant and the worker; whether Faraday notes that the check passed only after putting NULs back; a key entered as hex that Faraday writes under (it refuses a passphrase that is not printable ASCII), so keys of raw bytes are compared only when Faraday opens.

Vectors krux's test data for versions 5, 15 and 20 (tools/vectors/kef/): a CTR code under key, a GCM code under test key at 100,000 rounds, and the version 5 code opened by abc and by a wrong passphrase that passes its 3-byte check.

Random cases Each of the twelve versions sealed by Faraday and by krux, byte for byte for the ten that do not compress and opened by the other for all twelve, over entropy of 16 and 32 bytes, short and long text, text up to 1,024 bytes, text ending in NUL, text whose hidden check ends in 0x00, repeated blocks, ids of 0, 8, 252 and random lengths, every edge of the count, and wrong IV lengths; codes under a passphrase at 10,000 to 30,000 rounds, one of 200 characters with an id of 252 bytes, and keys of raw bytes (to 200 bytes) krux seals and Faraday opens; codes from a writer that skipped the NUL rules, with 1 to 8 NULs at the end; envelopes cut or changed; the suggested versions for each mode at every length to 1,024.

Differences KEF: Faraday refuses an empty plaintext, a compressed version over 1,024 bytes, an id of 253 bytes or more when reading (krux's unwrap does not check it), a count over 550,000 and a passphrase that is not printable ASCII when it works out the key, and a stream that inflates to over 102,400 bytes; krux does none of these. Each is asked of krux and counted. Faraday does not suggest a compressed version over 1,024 bytes.

KEF: a stream that inflates to exactly 102,400 bytes is read by Faraday and refused by krux's firmware (its read is capped at the limit and raises when it is asked for more before the stream has ended); one of 102,401 bytes or more is refused by both. A stream whose matches reach back more than 1,024 bytes is read by Faraday (any window to 32 KiB) and refused by krux's 1,024-byte window; Faraday writes none.

KEF: Faraday's unwrap refuses at once a payload that holds nothing but the IV, the exposed check and the hidden check; krux's unwrap takes it apart and its decryption then fails. Both end in a code that does not open.

KEF: version 7 (ECB with deflate) is refused for a repeated block by the side whose compressor makes a stream with one; the stream of the other has none, and that side's code is opened by both.

KEF: the compressed versions are not equal byte for byte, as Faraday's deflate and zlib's write different streams. Each opens the other's; krux's decryption inflates under zlib at wbits -10.

Secret handling

Reveal::KefCode

The GCM tag is compared in constant time by aes-gcm; the check bytes of the other versions are compared as Krux does; AES and PBKDF2 state nothing more.

The key, the passphrase bytes and the opened plaintext are Zeroizing values wiped on drop.

Limits

A written passphrase is printable ASCII of at most 200 characters; a read one is tried as typed, in NFC and in NFD.

A code that inflates past 100 KiB does not open.

A count over 550,000 is not written; PBKDF2 runs in steps of 5,000 rounds and stops when told.

Faraday's own calls

What Krux refuses to write is refused here, and a refusal names a version that works. Conservative, F219.

github.com/bitcoinpasada/faraday

Secret handling

Reveal::PaperForm

The GF(256) arithmetic of the shares and the RS1024 checksum are written without a table indexed by a share's bytes or a branch on them, as the code documents; a word is found by comparing its first four letters with every entry of the list in constant time (subtle), the rest of the word with the entry found, masked; the digest is compared in constant time (subtle's ConstantTimeEq); the code states no other timing.

The master secret is a Secret; the share values and points wipe on drop.

Limits

Secrets of 16 to 32 bytes of even length.

An iteration exponent above 5 is refused before any PBKDF2 round.

A group threshold of 1 over several groups is refused when splitting.

A wrong passphrase opens a different wallet: the passphrase is not a check.

Faraday's own calls

Shares with an iteration exponent above 5 are refused; a split writes exponent 1 with the extendable flag set. Conservative, F90.

A split with a group threshold of 1 over several groups is refused. Conservative, F90.

Secrets above 256 bits are refused. Conservative, F155.

The split's randomness is taken from the session's randomness, an answer for every 32 bytes; SLIP-0039 does not say where a split's randomness comes from. Neutral, F154.

Compared with SeedSigner's own encoders and DecodeQR (seedsigner/, unchanged, with embit's BIP-39 code in embit/); Project Nayuki's qrcodegen.py (qrcodegen/), module for module; segno 1.6 (python3-segno), an encoder of another lineage, at Faraday's mask and at its own; Pillow and CPython's zlib, which read every PNG Faraday writes; zbar (zbarimg) and zxing-cpp, which decode the QR code in every picture and return its payload as bytes (qr_decode.py).

Checked first: Its vendored files are hashed against references.sha256 before any run, and a published vector's answer is required of the reference as well as of Faraday; SeedSigner's reader is looser than Faraday (it takes 49 digits, a sign inside a group, 20 to 28 bytes, and does not check the checksum of digits), so Faraday's own rule, the lengths and the digits, stands in front of it in area_seedqr.py and the checksum is embit's; SeedSigner runs in English for every language, the indices being the same; the profile's own pictures are read from their pixels and must be Faraday's code module for module; segno is asked for Faraday's version, level and mode and its mask forced, and its mask is read back from it, its padding quirk being modelled in Nayuki's code; rqrr reads Faraday's and segno's codes; the self-test makes each decoder's answer wrong (a payload's last byte changed) and must catch it.

An empty payload, which segno refuses.

Vectors SeedSigner's nine test SeedQRs (tools/vectors/seedqr/); every string and picture of the Codex32QR profile (tools/vectors/codex32qr/), each decoded by zbar and zxing-cpp.

Random cases Keys of every length and language, both codes and the words read back; digits and bytes malformed; payloads in each mode at each level and version limit; 48-character codex32 strings in either case as Codex32QR codes and the pictures written of them read back and decoded by zbar and zxing-cpp, other lengths refused; the pictures of a key's SeedQR and CompactSeedQR decoded by both and read by Faraday to the key's words; greyscale pictures and QR pictures of random size and scale read by Pillow and zlib.

Differences SeedQR digits: SeedSigner reads a string with 1 to 3 digits more than 48 or 96 (it drops the tail) and one with a sign or a space inside a group of four (int() takes them); Faraday refuses both (5 cases, each checked on both sides and counted). SeedSigner takes no CompactSeedQR of 20, 24 or 28 bytes either, and strips checksum bits for 12 and 24 words only; the corpus keeps Faraday's 15, 18 and 21 word compact form on the entropy itself.

Codex32QR: Faraday picks the mask Nayuki's encoder picks; the profile's encoder chose another for 6 of its 22 pictures. For those the area swaps the mask of Faraday's code for the picture's with qrcodegen.py's masking, requires the picture, and counts it.

Segno 1.6 writes a zero codeword where the pad codewords begin when the data, terminator included, ends on a codeword boundary with room left (its write_padding_bits adds 8 zero bits where none are due; ISO/IEC 18004 7.4.10 adds none): its code is Nayuki's with that codeword changed, which rqrr reads, counted as a known difference, the padding; Faraday's is the standard's.

Segno picks a mask by its own penalty rule, and for some payloads another than Nayuki's and Faraday's; the area requires that code to be Faraday's under the mask segno reports (Nayuki's masking swapped to it) and rqrr to read it, and counts each as a known difference, the mask choice, which a reader ignores.

When it runs Before every release, with a new seed and about ten times the cases.

Recognise a secret in a file

SpecificationBIP 39 · BIP 93 · SLIP-0039 · 1 morePublishedCodeLibrary: bitcoin 0.32Library: sha2 0.11 (through core/faraday-crypto)Library: unicode-normalization 0.1 (through core/faraday-bip)Faraday's code: faraday/faraday-coreCross-checked withNot cross-checked
Action

Recognises a seed or a private key in a file, a scan or pasted text, works out the fingerprint of its key, and refuses a secret where one may not go.

Specification

BIP 39, Mnemonic code for generating deterministic keys, Deployed

BIP 93, codex32: Checksummed SSS-able BIP32 Seeds, Draft, vendored

SLIP-0039, Shamir's Secret-Sharing for Mnemonic Codes, Status not checked, vendored

BIP 32, Hierarchical Deterministic Wallets, Deployed

Code

Library: bitcoin 0.32.102, by the rust-bitcoin developers.

Library: sha2 0.11.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Library: unicode-normalization 0.1.25, by the unicode-rs developers, through core/faraday-bip.

Faraday's code: faraday/faraday-core: A words file is read in whichever BIP 39 word list it is in, checksum included; SLIP-39 shares and codex32 strings are gathered from their files and the codex32 seed is recovered from them. The fingerprint is that of the master key, with the passphrase a passphrase file or the person brings, and is kept by a memo keyed by SHA-256 of a tag and the secret, so the secret is kept nowhere. Pasted text is refused when it is words of any list, checksum or not, a SeedQR's 48 or 96 digits, an extended private key, a WIF key, a codex32 string or a SLIP-39 share; a scanner that loads a seed refuses only a private key.

Differences bech32 groups: a string that is not a segwit address of bc, tb or bcrt is read as bytes, all its data groups together, and the bits that do not fill a byte are dropped. BIP-173 has a padding rule only for a segwit address, so Core's convertbits, which applies it to any data, refuses some of these strings, and the area reads them as Faraday does.

bech32 length: Core's decoder refuses more than 90 characters (BIP-173); Faraday accepts any length the checksum covers. The area reads longer strings the same way.

Secret handling

Reveal::Bip85Child

The password's base64 is the base64ct crate's, which documents its encoding as constant time with respect to the data; its base85 is shown (§4.10).

The derived private key and the 64 bytes are zeroized before the function returns, and every value returned is a buffer that zeroizes on drop. The copies bitcoin makes inside derivation are freed unwiped, until the next lock (ESTABLISHED §4.8).

Limits

Applications 2', 32', 39', 128169', 707764' and 707785' only; no DICE, RSA or Nostr 128002'.

Hex is 16 to 64 bytes, a base64 password 20 to 86 characters, a base85 password 10 to 80.

An index of 2^31 or more is refused.

Faraday's own calls

Nostr keys by application 128002' are not built. Neutral, F27.

+ joins, upper case and a lightning: prefix) read by Faraday and by Core Lightning's decoder field by field and by the writer's own record, then one with a Bech32 character changed, one in mixed case, and three of thirty-eight spoils: types out of order or repeated, a field cut short or longer than the stream, a BigSize, truncated integer or feature field not minimal, a type outside the offer's ranges or an unknown even one, a text that is not BOLT #1's, an amount without a description, of zero, or a currency without an amount, no issuer id and no path, a path of no hops or a bad point, chains empty or of a wrong length, padding of more than four bits, a bad +, a wrong prefix, characters outside Bech32, and F232's stricter cases (a text over 4,296 characters, a non-zero padding bit, a chain twice or none known, a currency not in ISO 4217, an amount above 21 million bitcoin, an expiry past the year 9999, a first node byte that is no key, an unassigned character).

Differences BOLT #11 invoices: the package skips a p, h, s or n field of the wrong length, reads the first of a repeated p or s, and accepts both or neither of a description and its hash, mixed case, an amount finer than a millisatoshi and a leading zero value in x, c or 9, all of which BOLT #11 makes a refusal or says "should" of and Faraday refuses; it also accepts what BOLT #11 leaves open, which Faraday is stricter on: a repeated x, c, m, 9, d, h or n, a text over 1023 characters, an amount with a leading zero, and a required feature bit Faraday does not know; the area counts each refusal as known, naming its reason.

BOLT #11 route hints: the package reads a hop's fees and delta as signed integers (a fee above 2^31 reads negative); the area reads them modulo 2^32 and 2^16 before comparing, and keeps a hint to three hops, as the package drops the last hop of a hint of a multiple of five.

BOLT #11 fallbacks: the package reads only the first fallback address and writes the others in bech32 for every witness version, no bech32m; the area compares Faraday's whole list of fallbacks with the writer's f fields of versions 0 to 18, in order, and its fields of an unknown version by the writer's list.

BOLT #11 features: the package keeps one state per feature, so a feature with both its required and its supported bit set reads as supported only; the writer sets one bit of each pair.

BOLT #12 offers: Core Lightning's bolt12-cli passes the decoder no feature set, so it reads an offer with an even feature bit that Faraday refuses (BOLT #9 defines no offer feature); it also reads feature bytes with a leading zero byte, which BOLT #9 makes not minimal, and a description, issuer or currency holding a character of Unicode's Cc, Cf, Co, Zl or Zp categories, which BOLT #1 refuses and Faraday refuses; and it refuses what Faraday reads when the currency is missing from its ISO 4217 table (the list of 2018) or an amount in bitcoin has a first chain Faraday does not know (it names the unit by the first chain alone), which Faraday reads as BOLT #12 says; the area counts each as known, naming the reason, and every other difference fails the run.

BOLT #12 offers, F232's stricter cases: Faraday refuses what Core Lightning reads (a text over 4,296 characters, a non-zero padding bit, whitespace after a + that is not a space, tab or line break, a chain twice, no known chain, a currency not in the ISO 4217 list Faraday holds, an amount over 21 million bitcoin, an expiry past the year 9999, a first node that is no key, an unassigned character); the area requires Faraday's refusal and counts it as known.

github.com/bitcoinpasada/faraday

Secret handling

none: no secret leaves faraday-keys

AEZ's AES round is the aes crate's, which documents every backend as designed to run in constant time; the rest of AEZ is XOR, shifts and loops of fixed length, and the words are packed without a branch on their bits; the code states no other timing.

The deciphered entropy is held in a Secret that zeroizes on drop; the word bytes and the inner seed buffer are zeroized after use.

Limits

Version 0 only; a seed of another version or a failed checksum is refused before scrypt.

Reading only.

Faraday's own calls

aezeed and AEZ are written here; the cross-check asks LND's own Go aezeed package, over Yawning Angel's AEZ, the same words and passphrases and requires the same answers or refusals, once with the processor's AES round on both sides and once with the aes crate's software round against AEZ built without assembly. Neutral.

Action

Reads Core Lightning's hsm_secret, the plain 32 bytes, the 73 bytes encrypted under a passphrase, or the mnemonic form (a passphrase hash, then English BIP-39 words), or BIP-39 words as lightning-hsmtool generatehsm makes it, and gives the node key hsmd derives.

Specification

Core Lightning hsm_secret, Core Lightning's hsm_secret, plain or encrypted, and its node key, Convention

BIP 39, Mnemonic code for generating deterministic keys, Deployed

Code

Library: argon2 0.6.0, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: chacha20 0.10.2, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: poly1305 0.9.1, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: hmac 0.13.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Faraday's code: faraday/faraday-keys: A 73-byte file is a 24-byte header and 49 bytes of ciphertext; the key is Argon2id of the passphrase with Core Lightning's salt and libsodium's moderate limits, and libsodium's secretstream pulls one message of it; the node key is HKDF-SHA256 of the 32 bytes with info nodeid and a 4-byte salt counting from 0, retried while it is not a valid key. The mnemonic form is a 32-byte hash (zero without a passphrase, else the SHA-256 of the 64-byte BIP-39 seed) and English words in single-space form, the node key from the first 32 bytes of the seed; the words come from faraday-bip's BIP-39. Reading only; a file shorter than 32 bytes or longer than the mnemonic form can be is refused.

Written by Faraday

libsodium's crypto_secretstream_xchacha20poly1305 pull of one message (faraday-keys::hsm_secret) · No established implementation exists

No maintained Rust crate offers libsodium's secretstream; Faraday's is HChaCha20, ChaCha20 and Poly1305 of RustCrypto's crates, and is tested against a file libsodium sealed and against libsodium itself.

Checked first: LND's code reads the aezeed (wordlist, version, CRC-32C, scrypt, AEZ) and derives the node key, and its published answers (tools/vectors/aezeed/) are required of it as well as of Faraday; the Go program is built offline from the vendored tree (GOFLAGS=-mod=vendor, GOTOOLCHAIN=local) and its version is written into the stamp; the area stops when the program is missing; the software-round pass runs only on programs soft.py has checked to be soft (the tags noasm and purego; no AES-NI instruction in Faraday's command) and the command says it was built soft; ldk-node's derivation is written in the area from the sources the README quotes, and ldk's published answers are required of it as well as of Faraday; the bolt11 package's wheels and its stand-in are hashed against references.sha256 before any run, and each of BOLT #11's 31 published examples is required to be read by Faraday as the BOLT says (a valid one read, an invalid one refused), the package reading the valid ones to the same fields; Core Lightning's HKDF is its compiled code, its salt, limits and calls are those of hsm_secret.c, libsodium itself seals and opens the file, and Core Lightning's two published node ids for words are required of it as well as of Faraday; the area stops when the program is missing and the stamp records libsodium's version; Core Lightning's release archive is hashed against tools/reference/bolt12/release.pin by the fetch and again by every build, the area stops when bolt12-cli is missing, and each of the BOLT #12 vectors is required to be read by Faraday as the vector says (a valid one read, an invalid one refused) and read by Core Lightning's decoder to the same fields where Faraday reads it.

ldk-node's node key is compared with a derivation written here, not with ldk's code (Rust, not vendored): only ldk's five published answers are outside it; LND's key path numbers are written in the Go program from keychain/derivation.go, as LND derives through btcwallet, which is not vendored; the bolt11 package is not asked the fields it does not read (fields BOLT #11 does not define, a fallback of a witness version above 16, a second or later fallback), which are compared with the writer's own list; its signature check runs on btclib's curve, not libsecp256k1's, and refuses a high-S signature as libsecp256k1 does; hsm_secret.c itself is not compiled (it needs tal and libwally): its functions are written out in main.c, and for the mnemonic form libwally's two answers, whether the words validate and their BIP-39 seed, are python-mnemonic's, which takes 12 to 24 words and normalises the words and passphrase (NFKD) where libwally takes 27 and 30 words too and normalises nothing, so the area judges only English 12 to 24-word ASCII cases and Faraday refuses 27 and 30 words (F228); a NUL in the mnemonic form's words is not compared (Core Lightning reads the text up to it, Faraday refuses the file); the words' derivation (lightning-hsmtool generatehsm) is BIP-39's seed, whose first 32 bytes are taken by both sides here; Core Lightning's bolt12-cli reads one Bech32 string, so the area takes out a + between two Bech32 characters and the white space after it, and a lightning: prefix, before asking it, and a text with a NUL byte cannot be given to it (Faraday refuses it); its output is read as text (a short channel id as BxTxO/direction, chain hashes reversed).

Vectors LND's five cipher seeds, LND's two node keys, ldk's five node ids (tools/vectors/aezeed/); BOLT #11's 31 examples, valid and invalid (tools/vectors/lightning-bolt11/); BOLT #12's 53 offer vectors and 12 format strings, valid and invalid (tools/vectors/lightning-bolt12/).

Random cases Random BIP-39 seeds and entropies on every network; every aezeed case again with the aes crate's software round against LND's AEZ without assembly; random words, a wrong version with a right checksum, published seeds under a changed passphrase, a changed enciphered byte or salt with the checksum put right, a changed word, each refused by LND's code; 150 invoices written with every kind of field (amounts in every multiplier, description or its hash, payee key, expiry, final cltv, fallbacks of every version, route hints, features, metadata, fields BOLT #11 does not define) and signed, read by Faraday and by the package field by field, then each with one Bech32 character changed, with one letter in upper case, and with two of these spoiled: a repeated p or x, a wrong-length p, s, h or n, no p, no s, both or neither of d and h, an unknown required feature, a leading zero value in a longer x, c or 9, a leading zero or a fraction of a millisatoshi in the amount, a bad multiplier, an unknown network, a high-S signature, a field cut short, a text over 1023 characters, a description that is not UTF-8; for Core Lightning, random plain and encrypted hsm_secrets under random passphrases (opened by Faraday and by libsodium, node ids compared), a secret sealed by libsodium and opened by Faraday and by Core Lightning's functions, a changed byte, a wrong passphrase and a wrong length each refused by both, random mnemonic-form files with and without a passphrase (node ids compared; a wrong passphrase, a passphrase the file does not have and broken words each refused by both), and random BIP-39 words with a passphrase; 250 rounds of BOLT #12 offers, each an offer written with every kind of field (chains, metadata, a currency or an amount in millisatoshis, description, features, expiry, blinded paths, issuer, quantity, issuer id, unknown odd fields; + joins, upper case and a lightning: prefix) read by Faraday and by Core Lightning's decoder field by field and by the writer's own record, then one with a Bech32 character changed, one in mixed case, and three of thirty-eight spoils: types out of order or repeated, a field cut short or longer than the stream, a BigSize, truncated integer or feature field not minimal, a type outside the offer's ranges or an unknown even one, a text that is not BOLT #1's, an amount without a description, of zero, or a currency without an amount, no issuer id and no path, a path of no hops or a bad point, chains empty or of a wrong length, padding of more than four bits, a bad +, a wrong prefix, characters outside Bech32, and F232's stricter cases (a text over 4,296 characters, a non-zero padding bit, a chain twice or none known, a currency not in ISO 4217, an amount above 21 million bitcoin, an expiry past the year 9999, a first node byte that is no key, an unassigned character).

Differences BOLT #11 invoices: the package skips a p, h, s or n field of the wrong length, reads the first of a repeated p or s, and accepts both or neither of a description and its hash, mixed case, an amount finer than a millisatoshi and a leading zero value in x, c or 9, all of which BOLT #11 makes a refusal or says "should" of and Faraday refuses; it also accepts what BOLT #11 leaves open, which Faraday is stricter on: a repeated x, c, m, 9, d, h or n, a text over 1023 characters, an amount with a leading zero, and a required feature bit Faraday does not know; the area counts each refusal as known, naming its reason.

BOLT #11 route hints: the package reads a hop's fees and delta as signed integers (a fee above 2^31 reads negative); the area reads them modulo 2^32 and 2^16 before comparing, and keeps a hint to three hops, as the package drops the last hop of a hint of a multiple of five.

BOLT #11 fallbacks: the package reads only the first fallback address and writes the others in bech32 for every witness version, no bech32m; the area compares Faraday's whole list of fallbacks with the writer's f fields of versions 0 to 18, in order, and its fields of an unknown version by the writer's list.

BOLT #11 features: the package keeps one state per feature, so a feature with both its required and its supported bit set reads as supported only; the writer sets one bit of each pair.

BOLT #12 offers: Core Lightning's bolt12-cli passes the decoder no feature set, so it reads an offer with an even feature bit that Faraday refuses (BOLT #9 defines no offer feature); it also reads feature bytes with a leading zero byte, which BOLT #9 makes not minimal, and a description, issuer or currency holding a character of Unicode's Cc, Cf, Co, Zl or Zp categories, which BOLT #1 refuses and Faraday refuses; and it refuses what Faraday reads when the currency is missing from its ISO 4217 table (the list of 2018) or an amount in bitcoin has a first chain Faraday does not know (it names the unit by the first chain alone), which Faraday reads as BOLT #12 says; the area counts each as known, naming the reason, and every other difference fails the run.

BOLT #12 offers, F232's stricter cases: Faraday refuses what Core Lightning reads (a text over 4,296 characters, a non-zero padding bit, whitespace after a + that is not a space, tab or line break, a chain twice, no known chain, a currency not in the ISO 4217 list Faraday holds, an amount over 21 million bitcoin, an expiry past the year 9999, a first node that is no key, an unassigned character); the area requires Faraday's refusal and counts it as known.

When it runs Before every release, with a new seed and about ten times the cases.

github.com/bitcoinpasada/faraday

Secret handling

Reveal::LightningKey

Poly1305's tag is compared in constant time (subtle); the rest is not stated.

The passphrase, the Argon2id key, the secret and the node key are held in zeroizing buffers; the node key leaves only as hex for a reason that names it.

Limits

Reading only: an hsm_secret is never made and never loaded as a key.

A file shorter than 32 bytes, or longer than the mnemonic form can be, is refused. In the mnemonic form the words are English only, in single-space form with no NUL, newline or other whitespace; Core Lightning's text reading is stricter in no case and looser in some, which Faraday refuses.

Faraday's own calls

none
