Checked first: LND's code reads the aezeed (wordlist, version, CRC-32C, scrypt, AEZ) and derives the node key, and its published answers (tools/vectors/aezeed/) are required of it as well as of Faraday; the Go program is built offline from the vendored tree (GOFLAGS=-mod=vendor, GOTOOLCHAIN=local) and its version is written into the stamp; the area stops when the program is missing; the software-round pass runs only on programs soft.py has checked to be soft (the tags noasm and purego; no AES-NI instruction in Faraday's command) and the command says it was built soft; ldk-node's derivation is written in the area from the sources the README quotes, and ldk's published answers are required of it as well as of Faraday; the bolt11 package's wheels and its stand-in are hashed against references.sha256 before any run, and each of BOLT #11's 31 published examples is required to be read by Faraday as the BOLT says (a valid one read, an invalid one refused), the package reading the valid ones to the same fields; Core Lightning's HKDF is its compiled code, its salt, limits and calls are those of hsm_secret.c, libsodium itself seals and opens the file, and Core Lightning's two published node ids for words are required of it as well as of Faraday; the area stops when the program is missing and the stamp records libsodium's version; Core Lightning's release archive is hashed against tools/reference/bolt12/release.pin by the fetch and again by every build, the area stops when bolt12-cli is missing, and each of the BOLT #12 vectors is required to be read by Faraday as the vector says (a valid one read, an invalid one refused) and read by Core Lightning's decoder to the same fields where Faraday reads it.

ldk-node's node key is compared with a derivation written here, not with ldk's code (Rust, not vendored): only ldk's five published answers are outside it; LND's key path numbers are written in the Go program from keychain/derivation.go, as LND derives through btcwallet, which is not vendored; the bolt11 package is not asked the fields it does not read (fields BOLT #11 does not define, a fallback of a witness version above 16, a second or later fallback), which are compared with the writer's own list; its signature check runs on btclib's curve, not libsecp256k1's, and refuses a high-S signature as libsecp256k1 does; hsm_secret.c itself is not compiled (it needs tal and libwally): its functions are written out in main.c, and for the mnemonic form libwally's two answers, whether the words validate and their BIP-39 seed, are python-mnemonic's, which takes 12 to 24 words and normalises the words and passphrase (NFKD) where libwally takes 27 and 30 words too and normalises nothing, so the area judges only English 12 to 24-word ASCII cases and Faraday refuses 27 and 30 words (F228); a NUL in the mnemonic form's words is not compared (Core Lightning reads the text up to it, Faraday refuses the file); the words' derivation (lightning-hsmtool generatehsm) is BIP-39's seed, whose first 32 bytes are taken by both sides here; Core Lightning's bolt12-cli reads one Bech32 string, so the area takes out a + between two Bech32 characters and the white space after it, and a lightning: prefix, before asking it, and a text with a NUL byte cannot be given to it (Faraday refuses it); its output is read as text (a short channel id as BxTxO/direction, chain hashes reversed).

Vectors LND's five cipher seeds, LND's two node keys, ldk's five node ids (tools/vectors/aezeed/); BOLT #11's 31 examples, valid and invalid (tools/vectors/lightning-bolt11/); BOLT #12's 53 offer vectors and 12 format strings, valid and invalid (tools/vectors/lightning-bolt12/).

Random cases Random BIP-39 seeds and entropies on every network; every aezeed case again with the aes crate's software round against LND's AEZ without assembly; random words, a wrong version with a right checksum, published seeds under a changed passphrase, a changed enciphered byte or salt with the checksum put right, a changed word, each refused by LND's code; 150 invoices written with every kind of field (amounts in every multiplier, description or its hash, payee key, expiry, final cltv, fallbacks of every version, route hints, features, metadata, fields BOLT #11 does not define) and signed, read by Faraday and by the package field by field, then each with one Bech32 character changed, with one letter in upper case, and with two of these spoiled: a repeated p or x, a wrong-length p, s, h or n, no p, no s, both or neither of d and h, an unknown required feature, a leading zero value in a longer x, c or 9, a leading zero or a fraction of a millisatoshi in the amount, a bad multiplier, an unknown network, a high-S signature, a field cut short, a text over 1023 characters, a description that is not UTF-8; for Core Lightning, random plain and encrypted hsm_secrets under random passphrases (opened by Faraday and by libsodium, node ids compared), a secret sealed by libsodium and opened by Faraday and by Core Lightning's functions, a changed byte, a wrong passphrase and a wrong length each refused by both, random mnemonic-form files with and without a passphrase (node ids compared; a wrong passphrase, a passphrase the file does not have and broken words each refused by both), and random BIP-39 words with a passphrase; 250 rounds of BOLT #12 offers, each an offer written with every kind of field (chains, metadata, a currency or an amount in millisatoshis, description, features, expiry, blinded paths, issuer, quantity, issuer id, unknown odd fields; + joins, upper case and a lightning: prefix) read by Faraday and by Core Lightning's decoder field by field and by the writer's own record, then one with a Bech32 character changed, one in mixed case, and three of thirty-eight spoils: types out of order or repeated, a field cut short or longer than the stream, a BigSize, truncated integer or feature field not minimal, a type outside the offer's ranges or an unknown even one, a text that is not BOLT #1's, an amount without a description, of zero, or a currency without an amount, no issuer id and no path, a path of no hops or a bad point, chains empty or of a wrong length, padding of more than four bits, a bad +, a wrong prefix, characters outside Bech32, and F232's stricter cases (a text over 4,296 characters, a non-zero padding bit, a chain twice or none known, a currency not in ISO 4217, an amount above 21 million bitcoin, an expiry past the year 9999, a first node byte that is no key, an unassigned character).

Differences BOLT #11 invoices: the package skips a p, h, s or n field of the wrong length, reads the first of a repeated p or s, and accepts both or neither of a description and its hash, mixed case, an amount finer than a millisatoshi and a leading zero value in x, c or 9, all of which BOLT #11 makes a refusal or says "should" of and Faraday refuses; it also accepts what BOLT #11 leaves open, which Faraday is stricter on: a repeated x, c, m, 9, d, h or n, a text over 1023 characters, an amount with a leading zero, and a required feature bit Faraday does not know; the area counts each refusal as known, naming its reason.

BOLT #11 route hints: the package reads a hop's fees and delta as signed integers (a fee above 2^31 reads negative); the area reads them modulo 2^32 and 2^16 before comparing, and keeps a hint to three hops, as the package drops the last hop of a hint of a multiple of five.

BOLT #11 fallbacks: the package reads only the first fallback address and writes the others in bech32 for every witness version, no bech32m; the area compares Faraday's whole list of fallbacks with the writer's f fields of versions 0 to 18, in order, and its fields of an unknown version by the writer's list.

BOLT #11 features: the package keeps one state per feature, so a feature with both its required and its supported bit set reads as supported only; the writer sets one bit of each pair.

BOLT #12 offers: Core Lightning's bolt12-cli passes the decoder no feature set, so it reads an offer with an even feature bit that Faraday refuses (BOLT #9 defines no offer feature); it also reads feature bytes with a leading zero byte, which BOLT #9 makes not minimal, and a description, issuer or currency holding a character of Unicode's Cc, Cf, Co, Zl or Zp categories, which BOLT #1 refuses and Faraday refuses; and it refuses what Faraday reads when the currency is missing from its ISO 4217 table (the list of 2018) or an amount in bitcoin has a first chain Faraday does not know (it names the unit by the first chain alone), which Faraday reads as BOLT #12 says; the area counts each as known, naming the reason, and every other difference fails the run.

BOLT #12 offers, F232's stricter cases: Faraday refuses what Core Lightning reads (a text over 4,296 characters, a non-zero padding bit, whitespace after a + that is not a space, tab or line break, a chain twice, no known chain, a currency not in the ISO 4217 list Faraday holds, an amount over 21 million bitcoin, an expiry past the year 9999, a first node that is no key, an unassigned character); the area requires Faraday's refusal and counts it as known.

When it runs Before every release, with a new seed and about ten times the cases.

Secret handling

Faraday's own calls

BOLT #11 makes mixed case, an amount finer than a millisatoshi and a `c`, `x` or `9` field that begins with a zero value (the minimal form of zero is an empty field) a refusal, and Faraday refuses them. Where BOLT #11 leaves a case open, Faraday refuses the invoice: an amount with a leading zero, a repeated `x`, `c`, `m`, `9`, `d`, `h` or `n`, a malformed fallback of a version it defines, an empty route hint or a hop key that is not a curve point, an `n` key that is not on the curve, a non-zero padding bit, and a text over 1023 characters (what the Bech32 checksum guarantees). Conservative.

Action

Reads an OpenTimestamps proof and follows every path of its operations from the file's hash to its attestations, and says for each Bitcoin one whether it reaches the merkle root of a block header the person gives, whose hash meets its own target.

Specification

OpenTimestamps, OpenTimestamps proof files (.ots), as python-opentimestamps reads them, Convention, vendored

Code

Library: sha1 0.11.0, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: ripemd 0.2.0, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: sha3 0.11.0, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: sha2 0.11.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Faraday's code: faraday/faraday-ots: The proof's reader and the walk of its operations are written here; the hashes are the RustCrypto crates and SHA-256 is faraday-crypto's. A Bitcoin path is counted only when every hash on it is SHA-256, and the header's own proof of work is checked before it is used.

Written by Faraday

OpenTimestamps proof reader and walk (faraday-ots) · No established implementation exists

No Rust implementation of the OpenTimestamps proof format is established; Faraday's follows python-opentimestamps and is tested against that project's example proofs.

Area ots

Faraday's code faraday_ots (Proof::parse, Proof::verify, Header::parse), asked through the three requests ots.read, ots.verify and ots.header

Compared with python-opentimestamps' core modules, vendored unchanged in tools/reference/opentimestamps/, by the OpenTimestamps developers, on three small shims for what it imports and the repository does not vendor (Keccak-256, RIPEMD-160 over Bitcoin Core's pure-Python hash, and four names of python-bitcoinlib that only its printing routine uses); block headers are read by the area's own transcription of Bitcoin Core's SetCompact and proof-of-work test.

Checked first: The vendored files are hashed against references.sha256 before any run; the client's example proofs (tools/vectors/opentimestamps/) are read by both and the four that reach a block through SHA-256 and RIPEMD-160 alone are required to be committed by both; the shims' hashes are checked against known values before the corpus; each limit is built either side of its edge and both must agree.

The reference's printing of a tree and its stream readers; the order of a node's entries (the walk is compared as a set of paths); whether a header is in the chain; calendars, which neither side asks.

Vectors The OpenTimestamps client's example proofs (all 22, three of them invalid) and the headers of the six blocks they name, each proof walked against each header.

Random cases Proofs built through the reference's classes with every operation, the file hashed with SHA-256, SHA-1 or RIPEMD-160, side branches ending in pending, Bitcoin, Litecoin, Ethereum and unknown attestations, and chains to 255 operations, walked against a header that commits to the main path and one that does not; merkle trees of up to 40 leaves; proofs with a byte changed, inserted, deleted, cut or added to; every limit either side of its edge; headers over every kind of target and lengths other than 80.

Differences OTS: a Bitcoin path through SHA-1 or Keccak-256, or a file taken with SHA-1, is counted by the reference when it reaches the header's merkle root; Faraday names the first such hash and does not count it. Each is asked of the reference and counted.

OTS: an Ethereum attestation is verified by the reference against a block's transactions root; Faraday lists it by height and does not check it. A Litecoin one is listed by both (the reference raises when asked to verify it).

OTS: an attestation repeated at one node is collapsed by the reference and listed twice by Faraday.

OTS: Faraday refuses a proof over 64 KiB, a tree of more than 16,384 entries and a tree whose operations make more than 16 MiB of values; the reference reads each (a tree of 17 appends of one byte to a value of 4,095 bytes, each followed by 250 reversals, makes 17.5 MiB in 8.6 KB; 65 chains of 252 reversals behind distinct appends make over 16,384 entries in 17 KB).

Secret handling

none: no secret leaves faraday-keys

Not stated; a proof and a header hold no secret.

Nothing secret is held.

Limits

Reading only: no timestamp is made, upgraded or looked up; a pending attestation is listed with its calendar and not followed.

The header given is checked against its own target and not against the chain: a match says the file is committed to by that header.

An operation's argument or result over 4,096 bytes, a tree deeper than 256 levels, a height over 32 bits, a proof over 64 KiB, a tree of over 16,384 entries, over 16 MiB of values made by the operations in all, a header target above its network's limit and a proof with bytes after its tree are refused.

Faraday's own calls

A Bitcoin path counts only when the file's hash and every hash on it are SHA-256 or RIPEMD-160: a path through SHA-1 or Keccak-256 is named and not counted, where python-opentimestamps counts it. Where the reference leaves a case open, Faraday refuses: an Ethereum attestation whose payload is not one height, a block height over 32 bits, a number over 64 bits, a proof over 64 KiB, a tree of over 16,384 entries or whose operations make over 16 MiB of values in all, and a header whose target is above its network's proof-of-work limit (the reference reads these without a limit). Conservative, F230.

a wrong passphrase, a passphrase the file does not have and broken words each refused by both), and random BIP-39 words with a passphrase; 250 rounds of BOLT #12 offers, each an offer written with every kind of field (chains, metadata, a currency or an amount in millisatoshis, description, features, expiry, blinded paths, issuer, quantity, issuer id, unknown odd fields; + joins, upper case and a lightning: prefix) read by Faraday and by Core Lightning's decoder field by field and by the writer's own record, then one with a Bech32 character changed, one in mixed case, and three of thirty-eight spoils: types out of order or repeated, a field cut short or longer than the stream, a BigSize, truncated integer or feature field not minimal, a type outside the offer's ranges or an unknown even one, a text that is not BOLT #1's, an amount without a description, of zero, or a currency without an amount, no issuer id and no path, a path of no hops or a bad point, chains empty or of a wrong length, padding of more than four bits, a bad +, a wrong prefix, characters outside Bech32, and F232's stricter cases (a text over 4,296 characters, a non-zero padding bit, a chain twice or none known, a currency not in ISO 4217, an amount above 21 million bitcoin, an expiry past the year 9999, a first node byte that is no key, an unassigned character).

Differences BOLT #11 invoices: the package skips a p, h, s or n field of the wrong length, reads the first of a repeated p or s, and accepts both or neither of a description and its hash, mixed case, an amount finer than a millisatoshi and a leading zero value in x, c or 9, all of which BOLT #11 makes a refusal or says "should" of and Faraday refuses; it also accepts what BOLT #11 leaves open, which Faraday is stricter on: a repeated x, c, m, 9, d, h or n, a text over 1023 characters, an amount with a leading zero, and a required feature bit Faraday does not know; the area counts each refusal as known, naming its reason.

BOLT #11 route hints: the package reads a hop's fees and delta as signed integers (a fee above 2^31 reads negative); the area reads them modulo 2^32 and 2^16 before comparing, and keeps a hint to three hops, as the package drops the last hop of a hint of a multiple of five.

BOLT #11 fallbacks: the package reads only the first fallback address and writes the others in bech32 for every witness version, no bech32m; the area compares Faraday's whole list of fallbacks with the writer's f fields of versions 0 to 18, in order, and its fields of an unknown version by the writer's list.

BOLT #11 features: the package keeps one state per feature, so a feature with both its required and its supported bit set reads as supported only; the writer sets one bit of each pair.

BOLT #12 offers: Core Lightning's bolt12-cli passes the decoder no feature set, so it reads an offer with an even feature bit that Faraday refuses (BOLT #9 defines no offer feature); it also reads feature bytes with a leading zero byte, which BOLT #9 makes not minimal, and a description, issuer or currency holding a character of Unicode's Cc, Cf, Co, Zl or Zp categories, which BOLT #1 refuses and Faraday refuses; and it refuses what Faraday reads when the currency is missing from its ISO 4217 table (the list of 2018) or an amount in bitcoin has a first chain Faraday does not know (it names the unit by the first chain alone), which Faraday reads as BOLT #12 says; the area counts each as known, naming the reason, and every other difference fails the run.

BOLT #12 offers, F232's stricter cases: Faraday refuses what Core Lightning reads (a text over 4,296 characters, a non-zero padding bit, whitespace after a + that is not a space, tab or line break, a chain twice, no known chain, a currency not in the ISO 4217 list Faraday holds, an amount over 21 million bitcoin, an expiry past the year 9999, a first node that is no key, an unassigned character); the area requires Faraday's refusal and counts it as known.

When it runs Before every release, with a new seed and about ten times the cases.

Receive silent payments

SpecificationBIP 352 · BIP 392 · BIP 321 · 1 morePublishedCodeLibrary: bitcoin 0.32Library: secp256k1 0.29Library: sha2 0.11 (through core/faraday-crypto)1 moreFaraday's code: core/faraday-bipFaraday's own codeCross-checked withBIP-352's reference.pyOthers' code
Action

Derives a silent payments address, labels and scan key (BIP 352, 392) and finds the payments a transaction makes to them; reads and writes BIP 392's sp() descriptor.

Specification

BIP 352, Silent Payments, Complete, vendored

BIP 392, Silent Payment Scanning Descriptors, Draft, vendored

BIP 321, URI Scheme for Bitcoin Payments, Complete, vendored

BIP 353, DNS Payment Instructions, Complete, vendored

Code

Library: bitcoin 0.32.102, by the rust-bitcoin developers.

Library: secp256k1 0.29.1, by the rust-bitcoin developers (rust-secp256k1), over libsecp256k1, by Bitcoin Core's libsecp256k1 project (bitcoin-core/secp256k1).

Library: sha2 0.11.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Library: base16ct 1.0.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Faraday's code: core/faraday-bip: The scan and spend keys are taken at BIP 352's paths; a transaction's eligible inputs give the input hash and shared secret, and every output it pays to the wallet is found with the label it was paid to, up to K_max; the scan private key leaves only as BIP 392's spscan1q text, or the sp() descriptor over it with its key origin, for a named reason. An sp() descriptor, or its key alone after its origin, is read as a silent payments record: the scan key is read for its public key, in constant time, and wiped; an origin that is missing or not BIP 352's path on the key's network is refused, as are sp(KEY,KEY), spspend and a key with a derivation; a text that holds a scan key is a wallet file in Files, and one that holds a spend key a secret no scanner files. The app's check of a transaction takes its previous transactions one at a time and gives the previous outputs, in input order, once every one is known.

Written by Faraday

BIP-352 silent payments (faraday-bip::silent) · No established implementation exists

libsecp256k1's silent payments module is not yet in its Rust bindings.

Secret handling

Reveal::VaultEntry

Reveal::OutboxFile

A label tweak times G is libsecp256k1's ecmult_gen through a secret key, in a randomized context; the output tweak is treated as public and multiplied by ecmult, as libsecp256k1's own silent payments module does.

The scan key and the texts that carry it are written in fixed buffers that zeroize on drop. SecretKey is Copy, so every add_tweak, mul_tweak and negate copies the key and only the last copy is erased; the earlier copies are left in memory, later work under the security scope (ESTABLISHED §4.1).

Limits

Scanning stops at K_max, 2323 outputs for one scan key.

A script type the protocol does not list, a taproot input under H, an uncompressed key and a scriptSig holding no key matching its hash are skipped.

The wallet record keeps public values only.

Faraday's own calls

The faraday-silent 1 record holds the kind, the network, the key's origin, the label count and the address. Neutral.

BIP 174, Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction Format, Deployed

Vectors Every PSBT of BIP-174's, 370's and 371's test vectors (tools/vectors/psbt-bips/), with BIP-370's locktimes, read by btclib too.

Random cases Random version 0 and 2 PSBTs with every field Faraday reads, taproot trees among them, in random order, read field for field as Core reads them and written back byte for byte as read and as Core writes them, then broken one rule at a time; each version 0 PSBT made version 2 as HWI's convert_to_v2 and btclib's to_v2 make it, and back to its own bytes; BIP-370's locktime, transaction and version 0 form under every mix of required locktimes, also btclib's lock_time, tx and to_v0; one version 0 PSBT in eight carries fields btclib refuses and btclib is not asked of it.

Differences Version 0 made version 2: HWI's convert_to_v2 leaves out the PSBT_OUT_SCRIPT of an output whose script is empty, which BIP-370 requires; Faraday and btclib write it, and the rest of the PSBT must be the same.

Bitcoin Core reads a version 0 PSBT with a version 2 field as valid, the field as unknown; Faraday refuses it, as BIP-370 does, and so do HWI, which decides it, and btclib.

A taproot signature of 65 bytes whose sighash byte is 0, which neither Core nor HWI refuses, and bytes after a version 2 PSBT's last map or a stream that ends inside one, which HWI reads: Faraday refuses each, as BIP-341 and BIP-174 do, and so does btclib, which decides them (the stream ending inside a map checked, as the specification marked it not checked).

PSBT version 2 (faraday_psbt::v2): a BIP-370 key with key data is an unknown key; BIP-174's and BIP-371's fields inside are checked only when the PSBT is bridged to version 0, except a taproot signature whose sighash byte is 0, refused on reading. HWI checks them on reading; the area requires HWI and btclib to read the PSBT without those pairs, to Faraday's locktime and transaction. Where HWI reads a value shorter than its length says and makes a version 0 PSBT of it, which Faraday does not, Core must refuse the version 0 PSBT of the PSBT's own pairs, and btclib refuses the PSBT.

Btclib reads some PSBTs that Core and Faraday refuse (a key with key data on a field that takes none, for one): btclib is not asked to refuse what Core refuses, only what Core and HWI read and Faraday refuses.

Btclib refuses what the BIPs allow: an ECDSA signature that is not strict DER with a low S and an r that is a point's x, a sighash type of the seven it defines, a BIP-375 field in a version 0 global map, a previous transaction and a witness UTXO that disagree. About one version 0 PSBT in eight carries such a field, and btclib is not asked of it or of what is made from it. Pairs btclib does not write back as read (an empty final witness) and what it writes in their place are left out of the conversions it is compared on, and leaf hashes are compared sorted, as it writes them.

Action

Reads a version 2 PSBT as its key-value maps, checks BIP 370's shape and converts it to version 0 and back.

Specification

BIP 370, PSBT Version 2, Deployed

Code

Library: bitcoin 0.32.102, by the rust-bitcoin developers.

Faraday's code: core/faraday-psbt: bitcoin reads version 0 only, so the maps are read here. Every pair is kept as read and written back with what was set; a version 2 PSBT becomes version 0 once every output has a script, and only the signing fields (partial signatures, final scripts, taproot and MuSig2 signatures and nonces) are taken back from it. A version 0 PSBT becomes version 2 and back to its own bytes. The app reads a version 2 file wherever it reads a PSBT, signs its version 0 form and writes the version 2 PSBT that came in with the signatures added; where they do not go back into it, nothing is written or shown, never the version 0 form.

Written by Faraday

The PSBT version 2 reader (faraday-psbt::v2) · No established implementation exists

rust-bitcoin reads only version 0 PSBTs; its version 2 crate is pre-release.

About one version 0 PSBT in eight carries such a field, and btclib is not asked of it or of what is made from it. Pairs btclib does not write back as read (an empty final witness) and what it writes in their place are left out of the conversions it is compared on, and leaf hashes are compared sorted, as it writes them.

When it runs Before every release, with a new seed and about ten times the cases.

Action

Reads what a PSBT spends and pays: amounts, fee, verified change, warnings, and the wallet it defines for registering.

Specification

BIP 174, Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction Format, Deployed

BIP 173, Base32 address format for native v0-16 witness outputs, Deployed

BIP 350, Bech32m Format for v1+ Witness Addresses, Deployed

Code

Library: bitcoin 0.32.102, by the rust-bitcoin developers.

Library: miniscript 12.3.7, by the rust-bitcoin developers (rust-miniscript).

Library: sha2 0.11.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Library: base16ct 1.0.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Faraday's code: core/faraday-psbt: Change is verified only when the output's script is the address a loaded key's account, or a registered wallet, derives at the stated path; a claim on a loaded key that derives another script is a block. Warnings are ranked Info, Caution, Danger and Blocked. A wallet is offered for registering only when the PSBT's global xpubs give every script of its inputs and outputs. A PSBT's network is read from its global xpubs, else from the coin type of a BIP 44, 49, 84, 86 or 48 key path, else it is the session's. The signed-amount memory keeps the SHA-256 of the unsigned transaction and the amount each input states, and only when every input states one. Another device's signatures are merged only into a PSBT of the same transaction that asks the same sighashes, and are refused when one is invalid. The register sheet's hold registers a wallet only once its descriptor gives the spend's scripts and one of its keys is a loaded key's own at its path. An output over 21,000,000 BTC, outputs whose total is over it, or an amount an input states or their total over it, is a block, as Bitcoin Core's CheckTransaction and CheckTxInputs refuse them (`transaction::money_total`).

Secret handling

none: no secret leaves faraday-keys

Only public account keys are derived from a master key; the review compares public data. The library does not state the derivation's timing.

The review keeps public keys only; the derived private keys are dropped inside the master key's account_xpub.

Limits

Supported input scripts: p2pkh, p2sh-p2wpkh, p2wpkh, p2tr key path, and multi or sortedmulti in p2sh, p2wsh and p2sh-p2wsh, with miniscript and taproot trees through a registered wallet.

Multisig change is verified only by re-deriving it from a registered wallet.

A SegWit v0 input with no previous transaction in a transaction of several inputs is blocked.

Only a high fee and an absurd fee rate can be held past; every other danger and every block has no way past.

Another device's PSBT for another transaction, one that asks another sighash of an input and one with a signature that does not verify are refused, never merged.

An amount or a total over 21,000,000 BTC, in the outputs or the amounts the inputs state, blocks signing.

Faraday's own calls

Change under an unloaded key, or at a path under no loaded account, counts as a payment to others. Conservative, F136.

A script of several keys is signed only for a registered wallet that holds a loaded key. Conservative, F135.

A miniscript or a taproot tree of one key is signed only through its registered wallet. Conservative, F141.

A SegWit v0 input with only a witness UTXO in a transaction of several inputs is refused, which BIP 174 allows. Conservative, F155.

The signed-amount memory refuses one transaction stated again with other amounts. Conservative, F155.

Differences PSBT signing: Faraday refuses to sign a SegWit v0 input with no previous transaction in a transaction of more than one input; Core signs it, and BIP-174's own signer vector is such a PSBT. The refusal is ours, checked and counted. Faraday holds a finalized input to the same rule and refuses the PSBT when such an input is final, except a taproot one, whose final witness is the coordinator's.

PSBT signing, wallets: Faraday signs an input spent from a script of several keys (a multi of two or more, a miniscript naming two or more, a taproot script path whose carried leaves name two or more with its internal key, or are not its whole tree) only for a registered wallet that holds one of its keys and whose script it is; Core signs any. The area refuses, by a rule of its own, where no wallet the request registers holds a held key and gives the input, and counts it only where Faraday's refusal is that the wallet is not registered. A miniscript or a taproot tree of one key is signed only through such a wallet, and is otherwise left unsigned while the rest is signed (F141); the area takes Core's signatures off it. Half the corpus's multi, miniscript and taproot-tree inputs come with their wallet registered, so their signatures are still compared. A registered tree's every leaf has its wait met, since Faraday refuses a path that can never be valid, which the area does not work out.

PSBT signing: Faraday refuses a PSBT any input of which asks for a NONE or SINGLE sighash, and one that none of the held keys can sign: dangers no hold accepts (F136). Core signs the first and answers the second with nothing signed. The area expects both refusals by a rule of its own, counting a held key as taking part as Faraday's inspection does (a miniscript or a taproot tree only through a wallet in use), checks that Faraday's refusal names the danger, and counts them.

Taproot pkh leaves: Faraday signs a taproot leaf that checks its key by hash but does not finalize it: miniscript 12's finalizer looks the key up among the ECDSA origins and panics, and would push 33 bytes where the leaf hashed 32. Core finalizes such a leaf; the area takes the signatures under it off before Core finalizes, and counts each input Core would otherwise have finalized another way.

btclib's finalizer writes no taproot leaf that is neither a single key nor multi_a, and refuses to choose among leaves a PSBT signs: an input of another leaf is judged by Core alone (counted as a known difference), and btclib is given only the signatures of the leaf Faraday spent. It writes a plain multisig from the smallest m signatures on hand where Core and Faraday write the first m signers': btclib is given only the signatures Faraday's input carries, so it judges the script written from them and Core judges which were chosen.

Compared with Bitcoin Core v31.1 on regtest (core_node.py): descriptorprocesspsbt signs from the held masters' keys, finalizepsbt finalizes and extracts, testmempoolaccept judges each finalized transaction over its funding on the node; BIP-340's reference (secp256k1lab) and Core's key.py for the deterministic nonces, over Core's script.py sighashes; python-ecdsa (the distribution's package) and btclib (btclib/, its own curve) as a second curve lineage, beside them: every ECDSA signature again under plain RFC 6979 or verified, every BIP-340 signature verified and made again; btclib-wallet's finalizer (psbt.finalize with its miniscript solver) finalizes every input Faraday finalizes again and gives the same scriptSig and witness; for each sweep, btclib reads the WIF (scalar, compression, public key) and signs and finalizes the sweep on its own curve, and python-ecdsa makes the first-nonce signature of each input again, byte for byte; python-bip380 (miniscript/) reads the leaves. Faraday's refusals and the inputs a wallet's rule leaves unsigned are ours, in area_sign.py.

Checked first: Core is the pinned release, hashed against its pin before every run; the vendored files are hashed against references.sha256; a published vector's answer is required of Core as well as of Faraday; every ECDSA and BIP-340 signature Core makes is checked to verify under the hash the area computes before that hash is used for Faraday's deterministic nonces.

Vectors BIP-174's signer, finalizer and extractor vectors; the Core-built spends of tools/vectors/psbt/ (2-of-3 sortedmulti, the Liana wallet down both paths, a taproot tree by a leaf and by the key path, BIP 387's taproot multisig), signed by every subset of their keys; the finalizer vectors there (or_b's smaller signature, the taproot leaves that tie by count, the taproot multisig and MuSig2 spends).

Random cases PSBTs of one to four inputs, each spending a funding output on the node: P2PKH, P2SH-P2WPKH, P2WPKH, multi/sortedmulti in P2SH, P2WSH and P2SH-P2WSH, P2TR key path, P2TR script path (pk, pkh, timelocked keys, or_d, multi_a) with the key path beside it, miniscript in P2WSH and P2SH-P2WSH; held and foreign keys, cosigners' signatures already on (Core's), every standard sighash type, timelocks met and not; Core's signatures (ECDSA byte for byte, BIP-340 by verification and the deterministic nonce), each final scriptSig and witness and the extracted transaction Core's, the cleared fields, and every finalized transaction accepted by Core's mempool; an origin that derives another key refused; sweeps: a WIF key's P2PKH, P2WPKH and P2SH-P2WPKH outputs (P2PKH alone for an uncompressed key) spent beside another key's, signed by Core from the WIF and by faraday_psbt::sweep::sign, byte for byte, finalized and accepted by the mempool.

Differences PSBT signing: Faraday refuses to sign a SegWit v0 input with no previous transaction in a transaction of more than one input; Core signs it, and BIP-174's own signer vector is such a PSBT. The refusal is ours, checked and counted. Faraday holds a finalized input to the same rule and refuses the PSBT when such an input is final, except a taproot one, whose final witness is the coordinator's.

PSBT signing, wallets: Faraday signs an input spent from a script of several keys (a multi of two or more, a miniscript naming two or more, a taproot script path whose carried leaves name two or more with its internal key, or are not its whole tree) only for a registered wallet that holds one of its keys and whose script it is; Core signs any. The area refuses, by a rule of its own, where no wallet the request registers holds a held key and gives the input, and counts it only where Faraday's refusal is that the wallet is not registered. A miniscript or a taproot tree of one key is signed only through such a wallet, and is otherwise left unsigned while the rest is signed (F141); the area takes Core's signatures off it. Half the corpus's multi, miniscript and taproot-tree inputs come with their wallet registered, so their signatures are still compared. A registered tree's every leaf has its wait met, since Faraday refuses a path that can never be valid, which the area does not work out.

PSBT signing: Faraday refuses a PSBT any input of which asks for a NONE or SINGLE sighash, and one that none of the held keys can sign: dangers no hold accepts (F136). Core signs the first and answers the second with nothing signed. The area expects both refusals by a rule of its own, counting a held key as taking part as Faraday's inspection does (a miniscript or a taproot tree only through a wallet in use), checks that Faraday's refusal names the danger, and counts them.

Taproot pkh leaves: Faraday signs a taproot leaf that checks its key by hash but does not finalize it: miniscript 12's finalizer looks the key up among the ECDSA origins and panics, and would push 33 bytes where the leaf hashed 32. Core finalizes such a leaf; the area takes the signatures under it off before Core finalizes, and counts each input Core would otherwise have finalized another way.

btclib's finalizer writes no taproot leaf that is neither a single key nor multi_a, and refuses to choose among leaves a PSBT signs: an input of another leaf is judged by Core alone (counted as a known difference), and btclib is given only the signatures of the leaf Faraday spent. It writes a plain multisig from the smallest m signatures on hand where Core and Faraday write the first m signers': btclib is given only the signatures Faraday's input carries, so it judges the script written from them and Core judges which were chosen.

When it runs Before every release, with a new seed and about ten times the cases.

github.com/bitcoinpasada/faraday

Secret handling

none: no secret leaves faraday-keys

libsecp256k1 documents its signing as constant time.

bitcoin forces two copies of the key for Schnorr, the untweaked and the tweaked keypair; both are overwritten with secp256k1's non_secure_erase before the function returns, which the library calls best effort.

Limits

SIGHASH_DEFAULT and ALL are signed, and ALL with ANYONECANPAY after a caution; NONE, SINGLE and undefined types are refused.

A taproot input that no key of this device can sign is left unsigned.

A leaf is signed only when the leaf's script checks a signature against the key, read through the miniscript.

Faraday's own calls

aux_rand is zero, so a signature can be made again byte for byte; BIP 340 recommends fresh randomness against fault attacks. The library offers fresh aux_rand, and the app does not use it. Neutral, F156.

A miniscript or a taproot tree of one key is signed only through its registered wallet. Conservative, F141.

github.com/bitcoinpasada/faraday

Secret handling

none: no secret leaves faraday-keys

Every operation on a secret scalar is libsecp256k1's (SecretKey add, multiply and negate, and a nonce's public key). libsecp256k1's header says its code is written and tested to be constant time whatever the secret values; it states nothing of these functions by name. A hash is reduced to a scalar without a branch; the code documents no other timing.

A SecNonce is wiped on drop and consumed by the signature it makes; the session wipes its nonces when another transaction opens a session, and holds none once each has signed. SecretKey is Copy, so every add_tweak, mul_tweak and negate copies the key and only the last copy is erased; the earlier copies are left in memory, later work under the security scope (ESTABLISHED §4.1).

Limits

Key path only; a nonce or partial signature keyed by a tapleaf hash is a script-path spend and is refused.

The wallet must be registered; a participant set no registered wallet has is blocked.

Rounds across a lock, with the secret nonce kept in a vault, are not offered (F234).

Faraday's own calls

Each nonce's rand' is RFC 5869 HKDF-Expand of the session's seed, with the draw counter, the input's index and the participant's key as info: a fresh value per call, and a refusal when the counter would wrap. Neutral.

no decision

The secret nonce is held in memory for its one session and never serialised. Conservative, F234.

Checks every signature a PSBT or a finished transaction carries, finds a nonce used twice, recomputes this device's signatures and compares two PSBTs.

Specification

RFC 6979, Deterministic Usage of the Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA) and Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA), Informational

Code

Library: secp256k1 0.29.1, by the rust-bitcoin developers (rust-secp256k1), over libsecp256k1, by Bitcoin Core's libsecp256k1 project (bitcoin-core/secp256k1).

Library: bitcoin 0.32.102, by the rust-bitcoin developers.

Library: base16ct 1.0.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Faraday's code: core/faraday-psbt: Each signature is checked against the key it is under and the sighash the input's fields give, including the ones inside a finalized witness; one r or one R in more than one place is reported, under one key or several, and so is a point of a MuSig2 public nonce; a signature under a key this device holds is recomputed to say which nonce rule produced it.

Differences A partial signature that is not a strict DER signature with a defined sighash byte (or a taproot signature of 64 bytes, or 65 with a sighash byte that is defined and not 0x00): Bitcoin Core reads the PSBT and leaves the input unfinalized, Faraday refuses the PSBT or does not call the signature valid. Counted.

A final input whose script Faraday does not run (a hash time lock, which is no miniscript: a wrong preimage, the key of the other branch, a sequence below the lock, and its true spends; a P2SH puzzle; a segwit pk of an uncompressed key, which Faraday's segwit reading refuses, though a segwit multisig of such keys is read by hand and answers ok; a bare P2PK of a key off the curve; a taproot leaf of a version other than 0xc0, a taproot hash lock, a taproot leaf with OP_CODESEPARATOR or OP_DROP): Faraday answers unjudged, whatever the engine decides. Such a script reads not sound in the nonce check and is not refused, and only these rows may answer so: a miniscript or a multisig answering unjudged fails the area. Counted.

A legacy (bare or P2SH) multisig with a junk element below the dummy: consensus leaves it on the stack and accepts, Faraday refuses it. No wallet writes one, and the refusal stays. Counted.

What no wallet writes and no node relays, which consensus accepts: a P2SH redeem script or signature pushed by PUSHDATA1 where a direct push fits; a P2SH or_i selector 01 01 (a push of one byte, not OP_1); a P2WSH or_i selector [2] (not [1] or empty); an or_d dissatisfied by a wrong DER signature, not an empty element; an element left below a P2SH pk. Faraday's reading of the final fields refuses each, and the refusal stays. Counted.

A final input with a high S, or with a sighash byte no standard defines (0x00, 0x04, 0x05, 0x84), in a signature the script engine accepts under consensus's rules: Faraday refuses it (a mismatch, or an invalid signature) and consensus takes it. Faraday keeps to the standard here on purpose: a node relays neither, so a transaction carrying one does not reach a miner. Counted.

Secret handling

none: no secret leaves faraday-keys

Private keys are used only to recompute this device's signatures; what comes back is a verdict. The library does not state the recomputation's timing.

The keypairs made to recompute a signature are overwritten with secp256k1's non_secure_erase, which the library calls best effort.

Limits

A signature with no previous output to check against is not checked.

A signature under a sighash type that was not asked for is flagged.

A signature of another device is not recomputed.

A finalized taproot signature of 65 bytes with hash type 0x00 is reported invalid, key path and script path alike (BIP 341): it is a danger card, and the PSBT is not refused.

Faraday's own calls

The nonce check is run on signatures a device writes, comparing them with the RFC 6979 or BIP 340 nonce rule. Neutral.

Faraday's code faraday_psbt::sign (every held key selected, deterministic Schnorr, both RFC 6979 nonce rules) and faraday_psbt::finalize

Compared with Bitcoin Core v31.1 on regtest (core_node.py): descriptorprocesspsbt signs from the held masters' keys, finalizepsbt finalizes and extracts, testmempoolaccept judges each finalized transaction over its funding on the node; BIP-340's reference (secp256k1lab) and Core's key.py for the deterministic nonces, over Core's script.py sighashes; python-ecdsa (the distribution's package) and btclib (btclib/, its own curve) as a second curve lineage, beside them: every ECDSA signature again under plain RFC 6979 or verified, every BIP-340 signature verified and made again; btclib-wallet's finalizer (psbt.finalize with its miniscript solver) finalizes every input Faraday finalizes again and gives the same scriptSig and witness; for each sweep, btclib reads the WIF (scalar, compression, public key) and signs and finalizes the sweep on its own curve, and python-ecdsa makes the first-nonce signature of each input again, byte for byte; python-bip380 (miniscript/) reads the leaves. Faraday's refusals and the inputs a wallet's rule leaves unsigned are ours, in area_sign.py.

Checked first: Core is the pinned release, hashed against its pin before every run; the vendored files are hashed against references.sha256; a published vector's answer is required of Core as well as of Faraday; every ECDSA and BIP-340 signature Core makes is checked to verify under the hash the area computes before that hash is used for Faraday's deterministic nonces.

Vectors BIP-174's signer, finalizer and extractor vectors; the Core-built spends of tools/vectors/psbt/ (2-of-3 sortedmulti, the Liana wallet down both paths, a taproot tree by a leaf and by the key path, BIP 387's taproot multisig), signed by every subset of their keys; the finalizer vectors there (or_b's smaller signature, the taproot leaves that tie by count, the taproot multisig and MuSig2 spends).

Random cases PSBTs of one to four inputs, each spending a funding output on the node: P2PKH, P2SH-P2WPKH, P2WPKH, multi/sortedmulti in P2SH, P2WSH and P2SH-P2WSH, P2TR key path, P2TR script path (pk, pkh, timelocked keys, or_d, multi_a) with the key path beside it, miniscript in P2WSH and P2SH-P2WSH; held and foreign keys, cosigners' signatures already on (Core's), every standard sighash type, timelocks met and not; Core's signatures (ECDSA byte for byte, BIP-340 by verification and the deterministic nonce), each final scriptSig and witness and the extracted transaction Core's, the cleared fields, and every finalized transaction accepted by Core's mempool; an origin that derives another key refused; sweeps: a WIF key's P2PKH, P2WPKH and P2SH-P2WPKH outputs (P2PKH alone for an uncompressed key) spent beside another key's, signed by Core from the WIF and by faraday_psbt::sweep::sign, byte for byte, finalized and accepted by the mempool.

Differences PSBT signing: Faraday refuses to sign a SegWit v0 input with no previous transaction in a transaction of more than one input; Core signs it, and BIP-174's own signer vector is such a PSBT. The refusal is ours, checked and counted. Faraday holds a finalized input to the same rule and refuses the PSBT when such an input is final, except a taproot one, whose final witness is the coordinator's.

PSBT signing, wallets: Faraday signs an input spent from a script of several keys (a multi of two or more, a miniscript naming two or more, a taproot script path whose carried leaves name two or more with its internal key, or are not its whole tree) only for a registered wallet that holds one of its keys and whose script it is; Core signs any. The area refuses, by a rule of its own, where no wallet the request registers holds a held key and gives the input, and counts it only where Faraday's refusal is that the wallet is not registered. A miniscript or a taproot tree of one key is signed only through such a wallet, and is otherwise left unsigned while the rest is signed (F141); the area takes Core's signatures off it. Half the corpus's multi, miniscript and taproot-tree inputs come with their wallet registered, so their signatures are still compared. A registered tree's every leaf has its wait met, since Faraday refuses a path that can never be valid, which the area does not work out.

PSBT signing: Faraday refuses a PSBT any input of which asks for a NONE or SINGLE sighash, and one that none of the held keys can sign: dangers no hold accepts (F136). Core signs the first and answers the second with nothing signed. The area expects both refusals by a rule of its own, counting a held key as taking part as Faraday's inspection does (a miniscript or a taproot tree only through a wallet in use), checks that Faraday's refusal names the danger, and counts them.

Taproot pkh leaves: Faraday signs a taproot leaf that checks its key by hash but does not finalize it: miniscript 12's finalizer looks the key up among the ECDSA origins and panics, and would push 33 bytes where the leaf hashed 32. Core finalizes such a leaf; the area takes the signatures under it off before Core finalizes, and counts each input Core would otherwise have finalized another way.

btclib's finalizer writes no taproot leaf that is neither a single key nor multi_a, and refuses to choose among leaves a PSBT signs: an input of another leaf is judged by Core alone (counted as a known difference), and btclib is given only the signatures of the leaf Faraday spent. It writes a plain multisig from the smallest m signatures on hand where Core and Faraday write the first m signers': btclib is given only the signatures Faraday's input carries, so it judges the script written from them and Core judges which were chosen.

SpecificationBIP 141 · BIP 144PublishedCodeLibrary: bitcoin 0.32Library: base16ct 1.0 (through core/faraday-crypto)Faraday's code: core/faraday-psbtCross-checked withbtclib's Tx.parseOthers' codeFaraday's second version
Action

Reads a raw transaction, or a PSBT's transaction, to its txid, wtxid, weight and the previous outputs its source states.

Specification

BIP 141, Segregated Witness (Consensus layer), Deployed

BIP 144, Segregated Witness (Peer Services), Deployed

Code

Library: bitcoin 0.32.102, by the rust-bitcoin developers.

Library: base16ct 1.0.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Faraday's code: core/faraday-psbt: A raw transaction is read from hex or bytes by rust-bitcoin, and one it reads to no inputs is refused, as Bitcoin Core refuses those bytes (the segwit flag with no witness); a previous transaction is accepted for an input only when its txid is the one spent. The Decode screen takes the amounts its inputs spend from the spend's PSBT and the Inbox's PSBTs whose unsigned transaction is exactly the one decoded, and uses an input's amount only when no two of them state different ones. An output is named by its script kind (P2WPKH, P2WSH, P2TR, P2SH, P2PKH or OP_RETURN) and marked when it pays to a loaded wallet's first 100 addresses on either chain. A text is taken as a transaction in hex only when it has an even number of at least 120 hex digits that read as a transaction. Decode refuses a transaction with an output over 21,000,000 BTC or outputs whose total is over it, as Bitcoin Core's CheckTransaction does (bad-txns-vout-toolarge, bad-txns-txouttotal-toolarge), and one whose inputs' stated amounts, or their total, are over it, as its CheckTxInputs does (bad-txns-inputvalues-outofrange), so no total or fee it shows overflows.

Differences SeedQR digits: SeedSigner reads a string with 1 to 3 digits more than 48 or 96 (it drops the tail) and one with a sign or a space inside a group of four (int() takes them); Faraday refuses both (5 cases, each checked on both sides and counted). Codex32QR: Faraday picks the mask Nayuki's encoder picks; the profile's encoder chose another for 6 of its 22 pictures. For those the area swaps the mask of Faraday's code for the picture's with qrcodegen.py's masking, requires the picture, and counts it.

Segno 1.6 writes a zero codeword where the pad codewords begin when the data, terminator included, ends on a codeword boundary with room left (its write_padding_bits adds 8 zero bits where none are due; ISO/IEC 18004 7.4.10 adds none): its code is Nayuki's with that codeword changed, which rqrr reads, counted as a known difference, the padding; Faraday's is the standard's.

Segno picks a mask by its own penalty rule, and for some payloads another than Nayuki's and Faraday's; the area requires that code to be Faraday's under the mask segno reports (Nayuki's masking swapped to it) and rqrr to read it, and counts each as a known difference, the mask choice, which a reader ignores.

Vectors Coinkite's BBQr test files (tools/vectors/bbqr/): the 26 parts of a phone's scan, which read as a U file with the text Coinkite's test expects, and its ten PSBTs and transactions, each split in every encoding and read back to the file's bytes.

Random cases Files of every type and size written by krux (at the sizes of QR versions 1 to 20) and split by Coinkite in each encoding, read in any order, with repeats, a part missing, another transfer's part, a conflicting repeat and a part past the count, against Coinkite and krux; what Faraday writes, part for part krux's own writing at the same size, read back by join_qrs and by krux; numbered parts written by krux, written again by Faraday, read in any order against SeedSigner's decoder and krux and refused when malformed.

Differences BBQr: Faraday reads the file types P, T, U and J and frames of at most 4,096 characters; Coinkite's library reads every type BBQr defines and a version 40 part of 4,296 characters. Both refusals are checked and counted, and the corpus splits at version 39 at most. Faraday also refuses a set whose parts are not one length but the last, which Coinkite never writes.

Numbered parts: SeedSigner matches P and OF in upper case; Faraday does not (checked and counted). Faraday also refuses a part number of 0 or past the count, a count over 1,000, a repeat with other text and a part with no header, which SeedSigner's decoder files, fails on or takes whole; those refusals are written in the area, in front of the decoder.

Krux (checked and counted): reads the file types P, T, J and U only, decodes J and U as UTF-8 in 2 and Z only, stops at 160 KiB of characters (Coinkite's signed.txn is over it, in H), and can write a last part longer than the others, which Faraday refuses; its deflate reads a 1,024-byte window on a device, which the shim reads and writes. A set with an empty last part is read by Coinkite and krux and refused by Faraday, which refuses any part with no data.

Vaults

How the vault is built

SpecificationOwn specificationCodeSpecification · 3 actions

Two layers

A vault has two layers. The lock is the passphrase, Argon2id, ChaCha20 and HMAC. It is what keeps secrets safe. All of it is published, and each algorithm comes from an established library.

The plumbing is the code that lays the file out, reads it back and decides which field holds what. Most of what is Faraday's own is here. A bug in the plumbing usually means a file that does not open. The exception is in writing, under Security.

The file

A vault is one KDBX 4 file, the database format KeePass writes, under one passphrase. Faraday writes it in one shape and reads the shapes a KeePass app saves within limits.

The file holds a plaintext of a whole number of 32 KiB steps, from one step to 128 MiB, framed in blocks and wrapped in a header. A vault is as small as its contents allow, and no size is chosen.

The file's name ends in .kdbx. There is one passphrase and no slots: a file does not hide how many passphrases exist, because there is one.

The keys

The passphrase is put in Unicode Normalization Form C (UAX #15), and its UTF-8 bytes are hashed with SHA-256 twice to make KDBX 4's composite key. Then "é" typed as one character (U+00E9) and as "e" with a combining accent (U+0065 U+0301) open the same vault.

Argon2id version 1.3 (RFC 9106) stretches the composite key under the header's salt, memory, passes and lanes to 32 bytes; SHA-256 and SHA-512 over that and the header make the encryption key and the HMAC base, and each block has its own HMAC key.

Create a vault offers five memory steps, from 64 MiB to 1 GiB, each at 3 passes and 4 lanes. The lanes do not change the work a guess costs.

Sealing and opening

The body is the database's XML, padded to the file's size with line feeds and encrypted with ChaCha20, in blocks of 1 048 576 bytes each with its own HMAC-SHA-256 over its length and bytes. The header carries its own SHA-256 and HMAC-SHA-256.

The reader checks the version, the header's fields, the cost against its limits and the file's length before any memory is asked for, then derives the keys once. Every block's HMAC is checked before its bytes are used; a missing or extra block, a changed byte and a cut file are refused.

A seal writes the file again with a fresh salt, fresh IVs and a fresh inner key, all from one answer the caller draws, and a seal count one more than the last with the time.

A file a KeePass app saved with another cipher or KDF the reader takes, or other settings, opens, and its next seal writes it in Faraday's shape; only a format mark other than the one this build writes or a Meta that reads ambiguously holds a vault read only.

What it promises

Without the passphrase, the file shows its header, which states the cost and the salt, and a length that is a whole number of 32 KiB steps. Nothing in the body can be read or changed without the passphrase: the header's and every block's HMAC fail first.

What it does not promise

Offline guessing. Anyone with the file has its salt and cost and can try passphrases on their own computers. Each guess costs one Argon2id at the vault's cost.

Rollback. An older copy of a vault still opens. Someone who can write to the stick can put an older copy back; they cannot read or change anything in it. The seal count is how an older copy is told from a newer one.

A vault's size and its seal count are in the clear or can be read by whoever opens it; the cost and salt are in the header.

Independent review. Faraday's reader and writer are its own and have been read by pykeepass, keepassxc-cli and keepass-rs, in the vault cross-check area, over the files they write and the files those programs write.

Availability. A changed byte anywhere in the file fails its HMAC and the vault does not open; a backup is how a damaged vault is recovered.

What is Faraday's own, and why

The format and the algorithms are published. These pieces are not. For each: what it does, what could replace it, and why it is not taken.

KDBX reader and writer. Reads and writes the file vault: the header, the block stream, the cipher steps and the XML. Could be replaced by the keepass crate (keepass-rs). It drops the XML elements it does not model, which would disturb what a KeePass app wrote into the file, and it draws a save's randomness itself, with no way to pass the session's in. No audit of it is one Faraday's dependency checks trust. It is used in the tests as an outside reader and writer, never in what ships.

Faraday's names inside the vault. Decides which KeePass field holds a seed's words, a wallet or a GPG key, and keeps Faraday's settings in custom data under names that start with faraday. Could be replaced by nothing, since no standard puts a Bitcoin seed in KeePass. Unavoidable. An item the reader does not expect is named Unreadable and never used.

Padding after the XML. Keeps each file at one of its sizes, by adding line feeds after the XML's closing tag. Could be replaced by nothing, since KDBX has no padding of its own. It uses what XML already allows after its last tag, so a KeePass app reads the padded file as any other. A KeePass app that saves the file drops the padding.

OpenPGP code for the QR vault. Writes and reads the three packets a QR vault is made of. Could be replaced by rPGP (pgp) or Sequoia. Each brings every algorithm OpenPGP has had, with all the libraries those need, for a message that uses AES and OCB alone. rPGP has been audited by outside reviewers, but none of those audits is one Faraday's dependency checks trust, so each library it brings would be Faraday's own to vet.

HKDF (RFC 5869). Turns one key into others; in the vault only the QR vault uses it. Could be replaced by the hkdf crate. It leaves the intermediate key and each output block in freed memory unwiped; Faraday's own wipes them.

QR vault contents. The short TOML inside the code, padded to one length, holding one seed, share, passphrase or note. Could be replaced by nothing, since no standard exists for an encrypted seed QR that other tools read. Unavoidable. The cross-check reads the contents with an outside TOML parser.

Security

What protects secrets is all published. Someone with the file faces Argon2id at the vault's memory step, then the cipher. None of that is Faraday's design.

The main risk is parsing. The device reads files from outside, and a bug in a reader could crash it, hang it, or make it accept or refuse a file wrongly. The guards: a file's memory, passes and lanes are checked against limits before any memory is asked for; every block's HMAC is checked before its bytes are used; anything unexpected is refused, never guessed at; the XML reader refuses a DOCTYPE and an entity it does not know; each reader has a fuzz target; and pykeepass, keepassxc-cli and keepass-rs read what Faraday writes, and Faraday reads what they write.

The QR vault's reader checks the Argon2 cost against the same limits right after the key packet, before the data packet is read, and refuses every packet it does not use.

The one subtle risk is in writing. If Faraday's code reused a value it should draw fresh, a nonce for example, the file would still open everywhere, so the cross-check would not notice, but the encryption would be weaker. A library carries the same risk in its own code. The guard: every seal draws its bytes from one call for the session's randomness, and the specification counts every byte that call returns.

The library trade. A large audited library is more code that Faraday did not write and more to vet, looked at by others. A small piece of Faraday's own is less code and nothing extra to vet, looked at by Faraday, its tests and three outside programs. For one file format the small piece is taken, and keepass-rs would also give up two requirements of the file vault: that what a KeePass app wrote is kept, and that the session's randomness is the only source.

Key commitment. Every HMAC in a file vault is keyed from the key its passphrase makes, so no second passphrase opens the file to other contents.

OCB does not commit to its key. A QR vault someone else made could be built to open to two contents under two passphrases. Faraday makes every QR vault under one passphrase.

Later work. Faraday does not yet wipe every copy of a key left in freed memory, and Argon2id's later passes read memory at places the passphrase decides, which a program on the same computer could time. The device is offline and powered off after use, so both wait.

Opening it elsewhere

This shows the file is standard, and is not the way to use a vault. The cross-check opens a file vault with pykeepass, keepassxc-cli and keepass-rs, and Faraday opens what they write.

A QR vault is read by Sequoia's sq and by rPGP in the cross-check. GnuPG cannot read a QR vault: it follows LibrePGP, not RFC 9580.

Unlocking a vault on a computer that is online shows its seed on that computer. It is a last resort, for when Faraday is gone and the seed is needed back. Move the funds to a new seed afterwards and treat the old seed as exposed. The way to open a vault is Faraday on the offline device.

Passphrase strength

SpecificationOwn specificationCodeSpecification · 1 action

Words from dice

A passphrase of words drawn by dice from a list carries log2 of the list's length in bits for every word. Faraday has the three lists the EFF publishes (EFF word lists):

WordsEFF large list: 7 776 words, 12.9 bits a wordEFF short list 1: 1 296 words, 10.3 bits a wordEFF short list 2: 1 296 words, 10.3 bits a word
451.741.441.4
564.651.751.7
677.562.062.0
790.572.472.4
8103.482.782.7
9116.393.193.1
10129.2103.4103.4

The bits hold when every word is drawn by fair dice or by the computer's randomness, and not when a person chooses a word.

What Argon2id adds

Each guess costs one Argon2id at the vault's memory and passes, on the guesser's own hardware. Faraday states that work as log2(memory in KiB × passes) bits, which Create a vault shows beside each cost. The memory of the vaults Faraday makes ranges over a factor of 16, which is 4 bits; one more word from the large list is 12.9. The figure counts work, not how much more memory costs a guesser than time, and it gives no time per guess.

Other passphrases

A person may use any passphrase. Its strength is then theirs to ensure: Faraday does not measure a typed passphrase. A short passphrase, or one used anywhere else, is not protected by any cost.

Where to learn more

The EFF's page on dice-generated passphrases, eff.org/dice.

Arnold Reinhold's Diceware page, where the method began, theworld.com/~reinhold/diceware.html.

NIST Special Publication 800-63B, Digital Identity Guidelines, on what makes a password strong.

none: no secret leaves faraday-keys

Limits

Compared, for one part, with Faraday's second version, written by Faraday's authors in Python; that part is not checked against an outside source: the payload layouts of docs/VAULT.md §7, written in area_vault.py from that document; the KDBX file itself is read by pykeepass, keepassxc-cli and keepass-rs in the area (an outside reader each).

Area vault

Faraday's code faraday_vault's file (file::create, open and seal, the document model and the items of §7), its payload layouts and a passphrase's NFC form with the Unicode version it is made under, file::create_holding (an export), and faraday_crypto::argon2id

Compared with Pykeepass and keepassxc-cli (the distribution's packages) for the vault file, both ways, and keepass-rs for the file format only; docs/VAULT.md §7 written out in area_vault.py, over argon2-cffi and PyCA cryptography's Argon2id (OpenSSL's) (the distribution's packages) and Python's unicodedata, for the payloads.

Checked first: check_primitives runs before anything else: argon2-cffi and PyCA (44 or later over OpenSSL 3.2 or later, or the area stops) against tools/vectors/kdf/'s known answer; pykeepass and keepassxc-cli are the distribution's packages and the area stops and names a missing one, so a run without it fails; their versions are written into the stamp; the area stops where Python's Unicode is newer than unicode-normalization's.

keepass-rs does not count for the primitives and takes no part in the NFD or wrong-passphrase cases of files it did not read; the QR vault and OpenPGP are other areas.

Vectors The Argon2id known answer (tools/vectors/vault-primitives/); the export vector of tools/vectors/backup/, read with a byte changed refused, and with each bit of the version field and bit 44 of the Argon2 iterations changed refused; every file of tools/vectors/vault/, read by Faraday and by both outside readers.

Random cases Argon2id at small random costs and the costs it refuses; payloads made, read and malformed; passphrases in NFC, by case and at random; vaults Faraday writes at small costs with items of every kind of §7 and seals once more, read by pykeepass (every group, entry, field, protected mark and custom data item) and keepassxc-cli (listing and every field), under the passphrase, its NFD form, a wrong one and a changed byte; exports (file::create_holding) of one to eight entries whose Title, Notes and Password hold control characters, read the same way; files pykeepass makes at random (ciphers, KDFs, compression, tags, icons, custom properties, attachments, history, custom data) and keepassxc-cli makes (groups, entries, notes, attachments), opened in Faraday and sealed once more with nothing of the other program's lost; keepass-rs (format only, not counted for the primitives) reads the vaults Faraday writes and seals, with a wrong passphrase, the NFD form and a changed byte refused, and writes files (AES-256 or ChaCha20, Argon2d or Argon2id, compression or not, groups, entries, tags, icons, properties, attachments, custom data) that Faraday opens and seals once more.

Differences Pykeepass strips the characters XML 1.0 cannot hold from a protected value after decrypting it; Faraday keeps a Password's characters as they are put in (and leaves them out of a Title or Notes when it writes). The export loop expects pykeepass's reading of a Password and Faraday's own as put in, and counts the passwords that differ.

Pykeepass opens a file whose major version is neither 3 nor 4 without reading past it, deriving a key or checking a hash; KeePass refuses such a file, and the area counts a file as opened only when pykeepass read a KDBX 4 body (readers.open_kdbx). It also runs the key derivation the header states before it checks the header's SHA-256, so a changed bit in the Argon2 iterations (2^44 passes) holds it for good; KeePass and keepassxc-cli refuse at once, and the area asks pykeepass first with a key given and nothing decrypted.

The vault's passphrase is put in NFC (§3); KeePass apps do not. A vault under an NFC passphrase opens in Faraday under its NFD form and in neither outside reader. The area counts the NFD tries and expects exactly that.

Faraday's reader is stricter than the outside readers' in what it takes of a file (§4, §7.1): a block stream that ends before its empty last block (keepassxc-cli reads it), an XML document with an element after the root (keepassxc-cli), a protected value not canonical Base64, nesting past 64, another root element, a DOCTYPE and another encoding (pykeepass reads these). WIDER names each and the reader that opens it; the area expects exactly that set and counts those opens as known differences.

keepass-rs writes files Faraday refuses (§4): Twofish, AES-KDF and a Salsa20 inner stream (keepass_rs.REFUSED). The area makes one of each, expects Faraday to refuse it and counts the refusals as known differences.

KeePassXC 2.7.10 (and its development branch, November 2026) fails a save of a ChaCha20 file whose plaintext is a multiple of 1024 bytes, "Writing the database failed: Cannot process 0 length data.", and writes nothing: SymmetricCipherStream encrypts each full block of 1024 bytes as it fills and then the empty rest, which SymmetricCipher::process refuses (AES-256's last block is padded). Each save puts a random value of 128 to 1022 hex digits in the file (KPXC_RANDOM_SLUG), so it is chance, compressed or not, about one save in 450 at most. readers.Kpxc makes a command that writes again, once, from the file in a new shell, only on exactly that message and for a ChaCha20 file left byte for byte as it was; the save made again is judged as any other, a second such failure in a row fails the run, and each is counted as a known difference. The prelude shows the condition (kpxc_zero_length): on a file whose plaintext but for the random value is known (its ciphertext's length less the value pykeepass reads), 1500 saves that cannot reach a multiple of 1024 bytes do not fail, of saves that can, one must fail within 20,000, and the same file under AES-256 does not fail; when KeePassXC no longer fails, the run fails and the handling is to go.

keepass-rs decodes a custom data item's value as Base64 when it can, and the program encodes the bytes again (keepass-rs/src/main.rs). A value that is valid Base64 but not canonical (padding or trailing bits the encoder would not write) comes back as another text, so keepass-rs's reading of such a value differs from the file's and from pykeepass's. The area compares custom data as they are, so such a value is a known difference of keepass-rs, not a disagreement about the format.

github.com/bitcoinpasada/faraday

Secret handling

none: no secret leaves faraday-keys

The header's and every block's HMAC are compared in constant time (`verify_slice`); Argon2, SHA-2 and ChaCha20 state nothing more.

The keys are Secret values wiped on drop; the decrypted and inflated body are Zeroizing buffers; the passphrase's NFC form is wiped on drop.

Limits

Refuses a file longer than the largest vault takes, and one whose version, cipher, KDF or cost is not one the reader takes, before any derivation; a file of another length is not refused.

Refuses a file in which any block's HMAC or the header's does not verify.

A wrong passphrase and a file that needs a key file as well give the same refusal.

KDBX 3.1, AES-KDF, Twofish and an empty passphrase are named and refused.

Faraday's own calls

A file a KeePass app saved with other settings is opened and changed like any vault, and its next seal writes it in Faraday's one shape; it is held read only only for a `faraday.format` other than the one this build writes or a Meta that reads ambiguously (F190). Conservative, F190.

github.com/bitcoinpasada/faraday

Secret handling

Reveal::QrVault

Not stated; the seal is the message's.

The typed note and passphrases are wiped when the code is made; the random bytes and the key's or vault item's words copied into the job are wiped on drop, not lent.

Limits

A note holds the room the contents leave; a key of other than 12 or 24 English words is not offered; a vault item over the same room is refused with the reason, and a note with the characters to take off.

The memory step is one of the steps the message allows; a computer without the room for it refuses.

Faraday's own calls

A passphrase is typed twice and is not measured; the code is only as strong as it. Neutral, F190.

Link to this action

Open a QR vault

SpecificationRFC 9580 · RFC 7253 · RFC 9106 · 1 morePublishedCodeFaraday's code: faraday/faraday-keysCross-checked withSequoia's sq and rPGPOthers' codeFaraday's second version
Action

Opens a scanned QR vault code, or a chosen .pgp file, under a typed passphrase, and holds the one item it holds for the QR vault tool to say what it is and, behind an eye, to show a note or a passphrase; then offers what that item takes: a seed's words to the seed sheet, a share to the codex32 form, a passphrase added to the loaded key whose words make the key it names (with the offer worked out from fingerprints alone), and a note saved in the open file vault.

Specification

RFC 9580, OpenPGP, Proposed Standard

RFC 7253, The OCB Authenticated-Encryption Algorithm, Informational

RFC 9106, Argon2 Memory-Hard Function for Password Hashing and Proof-of-Work Applications, Informational

RFC 5869, HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF), Informational

Code

Faraday's code: faraday/faraday-keys: Reads the message of the action above with the typed passphrase after its stated Argon2 cost is checked against the limits (the app also checks the cost against the memory this computer has free before it starts the job, and names a code it cannot open at once), and reads the contents (`faraday-vault::contents`) into one held item that leaves `faraday-keys` only through the `Reveal::QrVault` reveals. The offers lend the held words or share once to the seed sheet or the codex32 form; `qr_passphrase_offer` makes the BIP-39 seed and BIP-32 master fingerprint of each loaded key with the held passphrase and returns only fingerprints, and `qr_add_passphrase` adds the key it finds; `qr_save_note` writes the note as a note record of the open vault.
