0.2.0 · faraday/faraday-keys/src/qr_vault.rs · QrOpenJob::run

github.com/bitcoinpasada/faraday

Secret handling

Reveal::QrVault

Not stated; the open is the message's.

The typed passphrase is wiped when the open ends, stops or fails; words or a share lent to an offer are wiped as the seed sheet or the form takes them; the item held is wiped on the next open, on leaving the tool, at the idle warning and at a lock.

Limits

A message Faraday does not open, or a stated cost outside the limits, is named before any memory is taken.

A wrong passphrase is told from a changed message and may be tried again.

No key loads with a stick plugged in; the card says so. A key already loaded is not added twice; a vault that is read-only, full or not open takes no note.

Faraday's own calls

none

Link to this action

Seal and open KDBX

SpecificationKeePass KDBX 4 · RFC 9106 · RFC 8439 · 3 morePublishedOwn specificationCodeLibrary: chacha20 0.10Library: aes 0.9Library: cbc 0.26 moreFaraday's code: faraday/faraday-vaultFaraday's own codeCross-checked withNot cross-checked
Action

Writes and reads the KDBX 4 container a file vault is: Argon2id (or, read only, Argon2d) over the SHA-256 of the passphrase's SHA-256, SHA-256 and SHA-512 key steps, ChaCha20 (or, read only, AES-256-CBC) over the body, HMAC-SHA-256 over the header and over every block of the stream, gzip read, and the inner stream's ChaCha20 over protected values. The store's functions listed here make the seal's job: the writes a seal makes from the records changed (a change the seal cannot write refuses it, never dropped), the UUIDs new entries and groups take from the bytes the seal draws (one fresh answer expanded by SHA-256 over a domain string, the answer and a counter: the UUIDs need to differ, not to be secret), and the check that the changes fit the file's size.

Specification

Own specification

KeePass KDBX 4, The KeePass database format, version 4, Convention

RFC 9106, Argon2 Memory-Hard Function for Password Hashing and Proof-of-Work Applications, Informational

RFC 8439, ChaCha20 and Poly1305 for IETF Protocols, Status not checked

RFC 2104, HMAC: Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication, Status not checked

FIPS 197, Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), Status not checked

RFC 1952, GZIP file format specification version 4.3, Status not checked

Code

Library: chacha20 0.10.2, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: aes 0.9.3, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: cbc 0.2.1, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: base64ct 1.8.3, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: hmac 0.13.0, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: quick-xml 0.41.0, by the quick-xml developers.

Library: miniz_oxide 0.8.9 and 0.9.1, by the miniz_oxide developers, a port of Rich Geldreich's miniz.

Library: sha2 0.11.0, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: argon2 0.6.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Faraday's code: faraday/faraday-vault: The container only, not the meaning of entries: signatures and version (4.0 and 4.1), the header fields (an unknown one refused), the KDF parameters' VariantDictionary with the cost checked against the vault's limits before any memory is asked for, the header's SHA-256 and HMAC, the HMAC block stream (every block's HMAC checked before its bytes are used, a missing or extra block refused), the cipher, gzip read into a buffer sized from its stated length and bounded by the largest vault, and the inner header with its attachments carried. KDBX 3.1, AES-KDF, Twofish, Salsa20 as the inner stream and an empty passphrase are named and refused; a key file or a challenge-response key is not recorded in a KDBX 4 header, so such a file cannot be told from a wrong passphrase (owner, 2026-11-02) and the wrong-passphrase message for a KeePass file says that a file which also needs one cannot be opened here. An Argon2 version missing from the parameters is a damaged file, as KeePass and KeePassXC take it. A file is written as Faraday writes one: 4.0, ChaCha20, Argon2id, no compression, 1 MiB blocks, the plaintext padded with line feeds to the size asked for; the master seed, IV, Argon2 salt and inner stream key are the 140 bytes the caller passes. The XML document (`kdbx::xml`) is read over quick-xml's tokenizer and refused, naming what was found, for a document not well formed, a DOCTYPE, an entity other than XML's five and character references, an XML declaration anywhere but the start, anything after the root other than XML whitespace, comments and processing instructions, nesting past 64, markup inside a text element the model reads, a Meta or Root missing or repeated, and a protected value that is not canonical Base64 (base64ct) of text; a comment or processing instruction is carried, and skipped in text the model reads; an entry or group with two UUIDs or a UUID of other than 16 bytes, a field with two values and the like is marked ambiguous and left as read, not refused; every protected value, those in carried bytes, history and the recycle bin included, is decrypted in document order and, on writing, the ones written are encrypted in document order under the new key from their plaintexts; what the model does not read is carried as the bytes read, and history and the recycle bin (the bin dropped while RecycleBinEnabled is True or absent) are dropped and counted.

Written by Faraday

The KDBX 4 container a file vault is: header, VariantDictionary, HMAC block stream, inner header and gzip framing (faraday-vault::kdbx) · Only the part used is written

Faraday writes only the part of KeePass's format the vault uses, over argon2, chacha20, aes and cbc, hmac, sha2 and miniz_oxide; keepass-rs, which no review Faraday trusts covers, drops the XML elements it does not read and draws a save's randomness itself.

Decision F190

0.2.0 · faraday/faraday-vault/src/kdbx/mod.rs · seal

github.com/bitcoinpasada/faraday

Secret handling

none: no secret leaves faraday-keys

The header's and every block's HMAC are compared in constant time (`verify_slice`); Argon2, SHA-2, ChaCha20 and AES-CBC state nothing more.

The composite key, the Argon2 output, the encryption key, the HMAC base and every block key are Secret values wiped on drop; the decrypted body, the inflated body, the document and the attachments are Zeroizing buffers, decrypted and unpadded in place; the Argon2 memory is overwritten before release. Not wiped: the SHA-256 and SHA-512 hashers' state, the ChaCha20 and AES-CBC cipher states and the AES key schedule, the inflater's own state, and the NFC normaliser's buffer of combining marks. The passphrase's first SHA-256 is a Zeroizing value; a seal works out the plaintext length before the buffer is grown, so a refusal as too small leaves no copy.

Limits

Version 4.0 and 4.1 only; KDBX 3.1 and older are named and not opened.

Argon2 version 1.3 with 8 MiB to 1 GiB of memory, 1 to 100 passes and 1 to 64 lanes, no secret key and no associated data; a cost outside is refused before any memory is asked for.

A plaintext of at most 4 MiB; a file too long to hold one is refused before any work, and a gzip body that states more is refused as soon as it is read.

The composite key is the passphrase alone; a key file or a challenge-response key cannot be told from a wrong passphrase (KDBX 4 records neither).

The passphrase arrives in Unicode NFC; the container puts it there.

Faraday's own calls

Only the part of KDBX used is written (F178, F190): the file is written in one shape, and a KeePass app's other choices are read. Conservative, F190.

Faraday's code: faraday/faraday-vault: The container is `kdbx::seal` (the `vault-kdbx` action); the seal count is one more than the last and the time is the caller's; a change the file cannot write refuses the seal and is never dropped; history and the recycle bin are dropped and counted; a vault under a cost below the first step takes the first step.

Compared with others' code: argon2-cffi (the Argon2 designers' reference code), for Argon2id, and Python's unicodedata, for the NFC form.

Compared, for one part, with Faraday's second version, written by Faraday's authors in Python; that part is not checked against an outside source: the payload layouts of docs/VAULT.md §7, written in area_vault.py from that document; the KDBX file itself is read by pykeepass, keepassxc-cli and keepass-rs in the area (an outside reader each).

Area vault

Faraday's code faraday_vault's file (file::create, open and seal, the document model and the items of §7), its payload layouts and a passphrase's NFC form with the Unicode version it is made under, file::create_holding (an export), and faraday_crypto::argon2id

Compared with Pykeepass and keepassxc-cli (the distribution's packages) for the vault file, both ways, and keepass-rs for the file format only; docs/VAULT.md §7 written out in area_vault.py, over argon2-cffi and PyCA cryptography's Argon2id (OpenSSL's) (the distribution's packages) and Python's unicodedata, for the payloads.

Checked first: check_primitives runs before anything else: argon2-cffi and PyCA (44 or later over OpenSSL 3.2 or later, or the area stops) against tools/vectors/kdf/'s known answer; pykeepass and keepassxc-cli are the distribution's packages and the area stops and names a missing one, so a run without it fails; their versions are written into the stamp; the area stops where Python's Unicode is newer than unicode-normalization's.

keepass-rs does not count for the primitives and takes no part in the NFD or wrong-passphrase cases of files it did not read; the QR vault and OpenPGP are other areas.

Vectors The Argon2id known answer (tools/vectors/vault-primitives/); the export vector of tools/vectors/backup/, read with a byte changed refused, and with each bit of the version field and bit 44 of the Argon2 iterations changed refused; every file of tools/vectors/vault/, read by Faraday and by both outside readers.

Random cases Argon2id at small random costs and the costs it refuses; payloads made, read and malformed; passphrases in NFC, by case and at random; vaults Faraday writes at small costs with items of every kind of §7 and seals once more, read by pykeepass (every group, entry, field, protected mark and custom data item) and keepassxc-cli (listing and every field), under the passphrase, its NFD form, a wrong one and a changed byte; exports (file::create_holding) of one to eight entries whose Title, Notes and Password hold control characters, read the same way; files pykeepass makes at random (ciphers, KDFs, compression, tags, icons, custom properties, attachments, history, custom data) and keepassxc-cli makes (groups, entries, notes, attachments), opened in Faraday and sealed once more with nothing of the other program's lost; keepass-rs (format only, not counted for the primitives) reads the vaults Faraday writes and seals, with a wrong passphrase, the NFD form and a changed byte refused, and writes files (AES-256 or ChaCha20, Argon2d or Argon2id, compression or not, groups, entries, tags, icons, properties, attachments, custom data) that Faraday opens and seals once more.

Differences Pykeepass strips the characters XML 1.0 cannot hold from a protected value after decrypting it; Faraday keeps a Password's characters as they are put in (and leaves them out of a Title or Notes when it writes). The export loop expects pykeepass's reading of a Password and Faraday's own as put in, and counts the passwords that differ.

Pykeepass opens a file whose major version is neither 3 nor 4 without reading past it, deriving a key or checking a hash; KeePass refuses such a file, and the area counts a file as opened only when pykeepass read a KDBX 4 body (readers.open_kdbx). It also runs the key derivation the header states before it checks the header's SHA-256, so a changed bit in the Argon2 iterations (2^44 passes) holds it for good; KeePass and keepassxc-cli refuse at once, and the area asks pykeepass first with a key given and nothing decrypted.

The vault's passphrase is put in NFC (§3); KeePass apps do not. A vault under an NFC passphrase opens in Faraday under its NFD form and in neither outside reader. The area counts the NFD tries and expects exactly that.

Faraday's reader is stricter than the outside readers' in what it takes of a file (§4, §7.1): a block stream that ends before its empty last block (keepassxc-cli reads it), an XML document with an element after the root (keepassxc-cli), a protected value not canonical Base64, nesting past 64, another root element, a DOCTYPE and another encoding (pykeepass reads these). WIDER names each and the reader that opens it; the area expects exactly that set and counts those opens as known differences.

keepass-rs writes files Faraday refuses (§4): Twofish, AES-KDF and a Salsa20 inner stream (keepass_rs.REFUSED). The area makes one of each, expects Faraday to refuse it and counts the refusals as known differences.

KeePassXC 2.7.10 (and its development branch, November 2026) fails a save of a ChaCha20 file whose plaintext is a multiple of 1024 bytes, "Writing the database failed: Cannot process 0 length data.", and writes nothing: SymmetricCipherStream encrypts each full block of 1024 bytes as it fills and then the empty rest, which SymmetricCipher::process refuses (AES-256's last block is padded). Each save puts a random value of 128 to 1022 hex digits in the file (KPXC_RANDOM_SLUG), so it is chance, compressed or not, about one save in 450 at most. readers.Kpxc makes a command that writes again, once, from the file in a new shell, only on exactly that message and for a ChaCha20 file left byte for byte as it was; the save made again is judged as any other, a second such failure in a row fails the run, and each is counted as a known difference. The prelude shows the condition (kpxc_zero_length): on a file whose plaintext but for the random value is known (its ciphertext's length less the value pykeepass reads), 1500 saves that cannot reach a multiple of 1024 bytes do not fail, of saves that can, one must fail within 20,000, and the same file under AES-256 does not fail; when KeePassXC no longer fails, the run fails and the handling is to go.

keepass-rs decodes a custom data item's value as Base64 when it can, and the program encodes the bytes again (keepass-rs/src/main.rs). A value that is valid Base64 but not canonical (padding or trailing bits the encoder would not write) comes back as another text, so keepass-rs's reading of such a value differs from the file's and from pykeepass's. The area compares custom data as they are, so such a value is a known difference of keepass-rs, not a disagreement about the format.

When it runs Before every release, with a new seed and about ten times the cases.

github.com/bitcoinpasada/faraday

Secret handling

none: no secret leaves faraday-keys

Not stated by the argon2, hmac or chacha20 crates.

The plaintext is a Zeroizing buffer, sized before it is grown so a refusal as too small leaves no copy; the keys are Secret values wiped on drop.

Limits

Refuses changes that do not fit the largest size, and names the bytes over and the next size.

Refuses a change the file cannot write, and keeps the vault open with its changes.

A vault held read only (a `faraday.format` other than the one this build writes, or a Meta or custom data that reads ambiguously) refuses every change and every seal (`Error::ReadOnly`); a KeePass app's other settings do not hold it read only.

Nothing is sealed before the session's answer has arrived.

Faraday's own calls

Each seal counts itself and stamps the sealing computer's clock in the file's custom data, so an older copy can be told from a newer one (F159). Neutral, F159.

Checked first: check_primitives runs before anything else: argon2-cffi and PyCA (44 or later over OpenSSL 3.2 or later, or the area stops) against tools/vectors/kdf/'s known answer; pykeepass and keepassxc-cli are the distribution's packages and the area stops and names a missing one, so a run without it fails; their versions are written into the stamp; the area stops where Python's Unicode is newer than unicode-normalization's.

keepass-rs does not count for the primitives and takes no part in the NFD or wrong-passphrase cases of files it did not read; the QR vault and OpenPGP are other areas.

Vectors The Argon2id known answer (tools/vectors/vault-primitives/); the export vector of tools/vectors/backup/, read with a byte changed refused, and with each bit of the version field and bit 44 of the Argon2 iterations changed refused; every file of tools/vectors/vault/, read by Faraday and by both outside readers.

Random cases Argon2id at small random costs and the costs it refuses; payloads made, read and malformed; passphrases in NFC, by case and at random; vaults Faraday writes at small costs with items of every kind of §7 and seals once more, read by pykeepass (every group, entry, field, protected mark and custom data item) and keepassxc-cli (listing and every field), under the passphrase, its NFD form, a wrong one and a changed byte; exports (file::create_holding) of one to eight entries whose Title, Notes and Password hold control characters, read the same way; files pykeepass makes at random (ciphers, KDFs, compression, tags, icons, custom properties, attachments, history, custom data) and keepassxc-cli makes (groups, entries, notes, attachments), opened in Faraday and sealed once more with nothing of the other program's lost; keepass-rs (format only, not counted for the primitives) reads the vaults Faraday writes and seals, with a wrong passphrase, the NFD form and a changed byte refused, and writes files (AES-256 or ChaCha20, Argon2d or Argon2id, compression or not, groups, entries, tags, icons, properties, attachments, custom data) that Faraday opens and seals once more.

Differences Pykeepass strips the characters XML 1.0 cannot hold from a protected value after decrypting it; Faraday keeps a Password's characters as they are put in (and leaves them out of a Title or Notes when it writes). The export loop expects pykeepass's reading of a Password and Faraday's own as put in, and counts the passwords that differ.

Pykeepass opens a file whose major version is neither 3 nor 4 without reading past it, deriving a key or checking a hash; KeePass refuses such a file, and the area counts a file as opened only when pykeepass read a KDBX 4 body (readers.open_kdbx). It also runs the key derivation the header states before it checks the header's SHA-256, so a changed bit in the Argon2 iterations (2^44 passes) holds it for good; KeePass and keepassxc-cli refuse at once, and the area asks pykeepass first with a key given and nothing decrypted.

The vault's passphrase is put in NFC (§3); KeePass apps do not. A vault under an NFC passphrase opens in Faraday under its NFD form and in neither outside reader. The area counts the NFD tries and expects exactly that.

Faraday's reader is stricter than the outside readers' in what it takes of a file (§4, §7.1): a block stream that ends before its empty last block (keepassxc-cli reads it), an XML document with an element after the root (keepassxc-cli), a protected value not canonical Base64, nesting past 64, another root element, a DOCTYPE and another encoding (pykeepass reads these). WIDER names each and the reader that opens it; the area expects exactly that set and counts those opens as known differences.

keepass-rs writes files Faraday refuses (§4): Twofish, AES-KDF and a Salsa20 inner stream (keepass_rs.REFUSED). The area makes one of each, expects Faraday to refuse it and counts the refusals as known differences.

KeePassXC 2.7.10 (and its development branch, November 2026) fails a save of a ChaCha20 file whose plaintext is a multiple of 1024 bytes, "Writing the database failed: Cannot process 0 length data.", and writes nothing: SymmetricCipherStream encrypts each full block of 1024 bytes as it fills and then the empty rest, which SymmetricCipher::process refuses (AES-256's last block is padded). Each save puts a random value of 128 to 1022 hex digits in the file (KPXC_RANDOM_SLUG), so it is chance, compressed or not, about one save in 450 at most. readers.Kpxc makes a command that writes again, once, from the file in a new shell, only on exactly that message and for a ChaCha20 file left byte for byte as it was; the save made again is judged as any other, a second such failure in a row fails the run, and each is counted as a known difference. The prelude shows the condition (kpxc_zero_length): on a file whose plaintext but for the random value is known (its ciphertext's length less the value pykeepass reads), 1500 saves that cannot reach a multiple of 1024 bytes do not fail, of saves that can, one must fail within 20,000, and the same file under AES-256 does not fail; when KeePassXC no longer fails, the run fails and the handling is to go.

keepass-rs decodes a custom data item's value as Base64 when it can, and the program encodes the bytes again (keepass-rs/src/main.rs). A value that is valid Base64 but not canonical (padding or trailing bits the encoder would not write) comes back as another text, so keepass-rs's reading of such a value differs from the file's and from pykeepass's. The area compares custom data as they are, so such a value is a known difference of keepass-rs, not a disagreement about the format.

Differences Where Faraday reads and pyotp refuses: a scheme, type or algorithm in other than lower (upper for the algorithm) case; a parameter name pyotp does not know, a counter on a TOTP, a label issuer that the issuer parameter does not repeat; Base32 with spaces or hyphens (a bare key) or = in the wrong place, or a length that Base32 cannot have. The area asks both about the URI with that difference taken out and requires the same answer, and Faraday's answer to the original to be that answer.

Where Faraday refuses and pyotp reads: a period over 3600 seconds (Faraday's rule), a parameter of the key URI format written twice or in a case other than lower or with a percent-escape in its name (pyotp keeps the last, or reads the decoded name), a parameter name with a tab or line break in it (pyotp strips them), a pair with no = or no value, a type with no / before its ?, a value written percent-encoded (Faraday reads it as it is), a fragment after the last value, a bare key of fewer than 16 characters, and encoder=steam, which pyotp reads as a Steam code of five characters and Faraday refuses, making no such code. The area asks both about the URI with a period, repeated parameter, name, pair or type difference taken out and requires the same answer; the percent escapes, the fragment, the short key and Steam's code are pinned one URI at a time.

Where both read and the keys differ: an escaped & or = in a value, such as an issuer's a%26secret%3DB. pyotp unquotes the whole URI first and reads a second secret from it; Faraday reads the value as written, one issuer and the key before it, which is the reading the URI's writer meant. Pinned one URI at a time, where the pin judges the kind and not the key.

HOTP: pyotp reads otpauth://hotp/ as a HOTP; Faraday refuses it, naming it HOTP (NotTotp::Hotp) and reading no code.

Times: pyotp works from a datetime, which ends in year 9999; past it the area asks generate_otp for the counter, time // period.

Action

Writes an image to a stick and checks it: the SHA-256 of the found image file against the release's image list before any write, of the decompressed bytes against the list as they are written, and of what was read back from the stick, with the stick's own IDs and name taken back out, against the list after; keep data takes a stick as the same build only when its boot partition's SHA-256 is the release's boot partition sum (F244).

Specification

FIPS 180-4, Secure Hash Standard, Status not checked

Code

Library: sha2 0.11.0, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: lzma-rust2 0.22.0, by hasenbanck (lzma-rust2), a port of the Tukaani project's XZ for Java.

Library: getrandom 0.3.4 and 0.4.3, by the Rand Project developers.

Faraday's code: faraday/faraday-payload: The image file is read whole and its SHA-256 compared before anything is written, then read again and decompressed into the writer; success means the writer received exactly the list's size with the list's SHA-256; a developer's image is hashed when confirmed and refused if it changed after; a Pi card is read back and compared with the stream as written, and the SHA-256 of what was read, with the card's own IDs put back where they went (docs/STICK-IDENTITY.md §4.3), must be the list's. A stick is made for its size, not copied (docs/STICK-IDENTITY.md §4.2): only the image's boot partition reaches it, byte for byte with the release's serial; its protective MBR, GPT (new disk and partition GUIDs from getrandom, the data partition to the last usable sector, every CRC-32 worked out again) and its data partition's FAT32 (faraday-fat's formatter, a new serial from getrandom) are written as regions and every region and the boot partition are read back and compared byte for byte; the GUIDs and serials are identities, not secrets. A stick made or keep data from a found image with no boot file signed first checks that the SHA-256 of the image's boot partition is the list's and writes nothing otherwise. Clearing the whole stick first writes zeros over every sector and reads none back. A name given the data partition (docs/STICK-IDENTITY.md §6) is faraday-fat's label write run over the sectors captured, each byte it changed a patch put back the same way.

bech32 length: Core's decoder refuses more than 90 characters (BIP-173); Faraday accepts any length the checksum covers. The area reads longer strings the same way.

Check Core wallet keys

SpecificationBitcoin Core wallet.datPublishedCodeLibrary: aes 0.9Library: cbc 0.2Library: sha2 0.11 (through core/faraday-crypto)Faraday's code: faraday/faraday-keysFaraday's own codeCross-checked withBitcoin Core (the pinned release's bitcoind on regtest)Others' code
Action

Checks each private key of a Bitcoin Core descriptor wallet against the public key its record names, and in an encrypted wallet opens the master key from the passphrase and each key with it; says pass or fail for each and gives nothing back.

Specification

Bitcoin Core wallet.dat, Bitcoin Core's descriptor wallet records and their encrypted keys, Convention

Code

Library: aes 0.9.3, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: cbc 0.2.1, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: sha2 0.11.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Faraday's code: faraday/faraday-keys: The master key is SHA-512 of the passphrase and the record's 8-byte salt, hashed again for the rounds less one (at most 10,000,000); its first 32 bytes are the AES-256 key and the next 16 the IV that open the 48-byte mkey under CBC with PKCS#7 padding. Each walletdescriptorckey is opened under AES-256-CBC with the double SHA-256 of its public key as the IV. A key must give the public key its record names (33 bytes, or 65 for an uncompressed key with its 279-byte DER), and in the clear match the stored hash of the public key and the DER. One mkey record is tried; a wallet with more is not whole. Where the keys are checked, each account key Core cached for a descriptor's key at a hardened step (a walletdescriptorlhcache record of 74 bytes) is derived again from the checked master key along the hardened path, one derivation for each account key, and must equal the cached bytes in constant time; a cached key whose depth, child number or parent fingerprint disagrees with its path, or is not a point on the curve, fails its record, and so does a cached key no master key was compared with, whatever the wallet's flags say.

Written by Faraday

Bitcoin Core's key from a passphrase and the opening of its encrypted keys (faraday-keys::core_wallet) · No established implementation exists

No maintained Rust crate offers Bitcoin Core's BytesToKeySHA512AES and DecryptSecret; Faraday's is SHA-512 rounds over faraday-crypto and RustCrypto's aes and cbc, tested against wallets Bitcoin Core made.

Decision F229

Checked against

tools/vectors/core-wallet

Computed by Bitcoin Core (the pinned bitcoind on regtest), run by tools/vectors/core-wallet/gen.py: plain, encrypted (passphrase faraday), watch-only, blank, labelled, imported descriptor and imported uncompressed key wallets, a multisig and a miniscript wallet of keys with further hardened steps, and a wallet Core's migratewallet made of a legacy wallet (its combo() descriptors, which Faraday lists and does not take), with Core's listdescriptors and getwalletinfo.

Area core_wallet

Faraday's code faraday_core_wallet::read_file (a wallet.dat read whole through faraday_sqlite, the records read and checked, the private keys checked in faraday-keys)

Compared with Bitcoin Core v31.1's bitcoind on regtest, offline: it makes each wallet (createwallet, encryptwallet, importdescriptors, getnewaddress with labels, generatetoaddress), says what it holds (listdescriptors and listdescriptors true, getwalletinfo), opens the passphrase (walletpassphrase) and loads or refuses a changed file (loadwallet).

Checked first: Core's release tarball is checked against its pinned SHA-256 (tools/reference/core/release.pin) before every run and the node's version is asked; every wallet.dat is one Core wrote and every answer is one Core gave of the same wallet.

Labels and the block locator (counted by Faraday; Core's address book is asked only for a purpose record Faraday refuses), the records Faraday counts and does not read, and the transactions themselves.

Vectors The three wallet.dat files Core made (tools/vectors/core-wallet/), plain, encrypted and migrated from a legacy wallet by migratewallet (made with the older release of tools/reference/core/legacy.pin), with what Core said of them.

Random cases Fresh wallets of eight shapes (plain, encrypted, watch-only, blank, with labels, with an imported descriptor, with an imported uncompressed key, with imported multisig and miniscript descriptors of keys with an origin and further hardened steps, a bare master key with hardened steps, and a hash before a key), with and without a transaction, each read with the right passphrase, a wrong one and none; and the same files with a byte flipped in a record, a record dropped or pages cut off.

Differences Faraday gives each descriptor as Core lists it (the account key from the walletdescriptorlhcache records, the master key's fingerprint and the hardened path as the origin, checksum included), and the area compares that whole text, with Core's listdescriptors without private keys, for every shape.

Faraday checks what Core does not look at when it loads a wallet: a private key's stored hash and public key, a descriptor's id and checksum, and flags and records Core's loader ignores. A changed file Core loads and Faraday does not call whole is counted, and must name a record and fault of the listed set; nothing is asked of Core there beyond that it loads, except where Core's own reading must show the condition: a purpose record Faraday cannot read (Core lists the address's purpose as unknown), a block locator that does not read as one (Core shows it read no locator from the record), a descriptor's range or next index out of order (Core lists it so, loaded with -keypool=1), and a header text encoding other than the three the file format names (SQLite reads it as UTF-8).

Core reads each transaction record as it loads and refuses a wallet one of which does not read; Faraday counts them. Core derives every index of a descriptor's range, and tops it up to its next index, as it loads; it refuses a descriptor that is not ranged whose stored range spans more than one index (the same script twice), and Faraday refuses it too; Faraday also refuses a range of 1,000,000 indexes or more and a next index of 1,000,000 or more (Core's limit on the size of a range). Past 2^16 the area does not wait for Core's answer (past 2^19 it takes minutes), and Faraday, which derives nothing as it reads, reads such a file whole up to that limit; it is counted where Core did not answer. Each is asked of Core in the prelude.

Core runs SQLite's integrity check when it loads a wallet and refuses a file in which a record's key was changed (the unique index beside the table still holds the old key), and refuses one whose walletdescriptorcache record was dropped; Faraday reads the table only, so it reads such a file whole when the changed key is still a record it accepts. Core also refuses a wallet whose block locator ends in another chain's genesis block, as it attaches the wallet to its node's chain; Faraday reads no chain and does not read the locator's hashes. Each is asked of Core in the prelude.

Faraday refuses a wallet of another network than its mode and a file with a journal, log or lock beside it, which Core opens (and recovers); the area reads regtest wallets with nothing beside them, so neither arises.

Differences BIP-375: Faraday takes a key a PSBT states for a P2PKH, P2SH-P2WPKH or P2WPKH input only where the input's script commits to it (F89); the validator takes the first key stated, so a PSBT it accepts with an unbound key is refused by Faraday.

BIP-375: Faraday accepts the scripts of a scan key's outputs numbered in sorted order of their spend keys, as the BIP's text says, and in output order, as its vectors do; the validator accepts output order only.

BIP-375: Faraday refuses an input whose redeem script is not the one its P2SH script hashes, and one whose previous transaction is not the one spent; the validator reads both fields without checking them.

BIP-375: btclib-wallet takes a taproot input's NUMS internal key as a reason to skip the input only against a proof (a merkle root or a control block that tweaks the NUMS point to the output key), and counts the input otherwise; Faraday and the validator skip on the claim. A PSBT with an unproved claim is not asked of btclib-wallet; the run prints how many PSBTs it judged and how many it was not asked. A proved claim only in a control block, with no internal key set, is not detected: btclib-wallet would skip the input, Faraday would count it, and the run would stop on it. The corpus also makes inputs whose claim is proved, which all three skip.

github.com/bitcoinpasada/faraday

Secret handling

none: no secret leaves faraday-keys

The output tweak is treated as public and multiplied by ecmult, as libsecp256k1's own silent payments module does.

The secret's bytes and the hashes they pass through are zeroized before return; each private key used is erased before its input is done. The nonce is a SecretScalar, erased when it is dropped, but musig.rs's `match (self.0, other.0)`, `self.0.map` and `self.0.and_then` leave copies of it. SecretKey is Copy, so every add_tweak, mul_tweak and negate copies the key and only the last copy is erased; the earlier copies are left in memory, later work under the security scope (ESTABLISHED §4.1).

Limits

Built in core and not reachable from the app: the device does not send.

An eligible input whose public key the PSBT does not state, a P2SH input with no redeem script and a previous transaction that is not the one spent stop the check.

A SegWit version above 1 and a sighash other than ALL are refused.

Faraday's own calls

A key a PSBT states for an input counts only where the input's script commits to it, which is stricter than BIP 375's reference validator. Conservative, F89.

Spends of SegWit above v1 and sighashes other than ALL are refused. Conservative.

Read the items inside a vault

SpecificationTOML v1.0.0PublishedCodeLibrary: toml_parser 1.1Library: pem-rfc7468 1.0Library: base16ct 1.0 (through core/faraday-crypto)Faraday's code: faraday/faraday-vaultFaraday's own codeCross-checked withNot cross-checked
Action

Reads the TOML a vault holds into its items: the keys of a QR vault (a seed's words, a codex32 share, a passphrase, a note, or nothing), and the three TOML values a file vault keeps in its custom data (a backup plan, a seed's codex32 facts, its BIP-85 facts). What the Spec does not name is refused: a syntax refusal names the line and every other the key; a value read is written again to the same fields. A file vault's KDBX document is mapped to the records the app reads and back (`kdbx::items`): each Faraday item by its `faraday.kind` in its published text form (BIP-39 words of a list or a seed in hex, a BIP-388 policy or a descriptor, PEM keys and certificates, an armored GPG key, a codex32 string), a person's entry by its six fields, and the database's format, seal count, plans and signed amounts; an item that does not read is named Unreadable, never made a record, and written back as read.

Specification

TOML v1.0.0, TOML, Tom's Obvious Minimal Language, version 1.0.0, Status not checked

Code

Library: toml_parser 1.1.3+spec-1.1.0, by the toml-rs developers.

Library: pem-rfc7468 1.0.0, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: base16ct 1.0.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Faraday's code: faraday/faraday-vault: The parser alone reads TOML v1.0.0 tokens; the tree, the duplicate rules, the key and size limits of docs/VAULT.md sections 2.1 and 7 and the values' meaning are Faraday's own (`contents.rs`, `contents/tree.rs`). Whatever is outside those rules is refused by name. The KDBX mapping (`kdbx/items/`) is Faraday's own over the document model, faraday-bip's BIP-39, wallet policy, descriptor and codex32 readers, the TOTP reader and pem-rfc7468: the field names, the kinds, the labels of related secrets (several shares of one threshold, identifier, index and key) and the Unreadable items of docs/VAULT.md section 7.

Written by Faraday

toml_parser reads the tokens; Faraday builds the tree and refuses what VAULT.md does not name, as the JSON visitor does over serde_json.

github.com/bitcoinpasada/faraday

Secret handling

none: no secret leaves faraday-keys

The reader branches on secret text (a seed's words, a passphrase, a note) while it parses, and so does the KDBX mapping over an item's fields; constant-time parsing is later work (docs/SECURITY-MODEL.md, the security scope).

The text read and the values made from it are held in wiping types (docs/KEYS.md); what toml_parser and the word-list parser keep is not wiped (docs/deps/toml_parser.md). The KDBX mapping's words, seed hex and PEM keys are made in wiping buffers (`kdbx/items/forms.rs`); a GPG key's armored text is held in a wiping string.

Limits

A QR vault is exactly 226 bytes; a plan over 1 MiB, an inline table over its size, a key part of more than 128 bytes, a key path of more than 8 parts and a key outside docs/VAULT.md sections 2.1 and 7 are refused.

A QR vault holds one item, a note of at most QR_NOTE_MAX bytes and a passphrase of at most QR_PASSPHRASE_MAX; more is refused as too long, naming the key.

Faraday's own calls

Nothing about Faraday's items refuses a KDBX file: an item that does not read is named Unreadable, by its title, UUID, field and fault, is never made a record and is written back as read; a faraday.format other than 1 makes the vault read-only (owner, 2026-11-03; docs/VAULT.md section 7). Conservative, F194.

Whatever the Spec's TOML does not name is refused, so a value that adds a key is not read (F190 point 3, docs/VAULT.md section 7). Conservative, F194.

A QR vault's contents are the item's keys at the top of a TOML document, padded to 226 bytes with line feeds (F190 point 5, docs/VAULT.md section 2.1). Neutral, F194.

Seal a QR vault's OpenPGP message

SpecificationRFC 9580 · RFC 7253 · RFC 9106 · 1 morePublishedCodeLibrary: aes 0.9Library: ocb3 0.2Library: argon2 0.6 (through core/faraday-crypto)Faraday's code: faraday/faraday-pgpFaraday's own codeCross-checked withSequoia's sqOthers' codeFaraday's second version
Action

Writes and reads an RFC 9580 message under a passphrase: Argon2id (the Argon2 S2K, 3 passes, 4 lanes) over the passphrase gives a key, HKDF-SHA-256 makes the key that AES-256-OCB wraps the session key with in a version 6 symmetric-key encrypted session key packet, and a version 2 data packet holds one literal data packet in AES-256-OCB chunks under a key HKDF-SHA-256 makes from the session key and a 32-byte salt, with a final tag over the plaintext's length.

Specification

RFC 9580, OpenPGP, Proposed Standard

RFC 7253, The OCB Authenticated-Encryption Algorithm, Informational

RFC 9106, Argon2 Memory-Hard Function for Password Hashing and Proof-of-Work Applications, Informational

RFC 5869, HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF), Informational

Code

Library: aes 0.9.3, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: ocb3 0.2.0, by the RustCrypto developers.

Library: argon2 0.6.0, by the RustCrypto developers, through core/faraday-crypto.

Faraday's code: faraday/faraday-pgp: Only the part used is written: the version 6 symmetric-key packet with the Argon2 S2K and the version 2 data packet, both AES-256 and OCB, and the one literal data packet, in any length form RFC 9580 allows. The Argon2 cost is checked against the limits right after the key packet, before the data packet is read or any Argon2 memory is taken, padding packets are ignored, every tag is checked before plaintext is returned, and every other packet, version, algorithm or trailing byte is named and not opened. HKDF-SHA-256 is Faraday's own (`faraday-crypto`); Argon2id, AES and OCB are the RustCrypto crates.

Written by Faraday

HKDF-SHA256, one copy (faraday-crypto::hash) · One exists but does not fit Faraday's rules for keys

The Rust HKDF library leaves the pseudorandom key and its output blocks unwiped; Faraday's holds both in buffers it wipes.

Does not fit: hkdf 0.13.0 returns the pseudorandom key and leaves each output block T(i) in plain arrays it does not wipe

Decision F180

The QR vault's OpenPGP message: the version 6 symmetric-key packet with the Argon2 S2K, the version 2 data packet and the literal data packet (faraday-pgp::message) · Only the part used is written

Faraday writes only the three packets a QR vault uses, over argon2, aes and ocb3 and Faraday's HKDF; rPGP, which no review Faraday trusts covers, brings every OpenPGP algorithm.

Decision F190

tools/vectors/openpgp

Published, by RFC 9580 Appendix A (A.10, the version 6 symmetric-key session key and the version 2 data packet with AES-128 and OCB; A.12.3, the Argon2 S2K with AES-256), made by the RFC's authors.

Faraday's code faraday_vault::qr (the QR vault sealed and opened, with faraday_pgp::message)

Compared with Sequoia's sq, the distribution's package, over Nettle (judges the primitives except Argon2, which it shares with the app's lineage); rPGP (tools/crosscheck/rpgp/, a program outside the workspace, on RustCrypto like the app: judges the format only); PyCA cryptography's Argon2id, HKDF-SHA-256 and AES-256-OCB (OpenSSL's), which judge the primitives, under the OpenPGP framing written in the area from RFC 9580 and docs/VAULT.md §1.2 (Faraday's second version, not another program's); the QR TOML qr_toml written in the area from §2.1, each opened item also read by CPython's tomllib.

Checked first: Sq is the distribution's package, built over Nettle (the run stops otherwise, judges.py), its version written into the stamp; rPGP is built from the crates.io release tools/crosscheck/rpgp/Cargo.lock names; PyCA must be 44 or later over OpenSSL 3.2 or later or the area stops, and its Argon2id, HKDF-SHA-256 and AES-OCB are checked against the repository's Argon2id known answer, RFC 5869 test case 1 and RFC 7253's first vector first; sq and rPGP open the repository's vault vectors, and so does the PyCA judge, which reads strictly and refuses anything but a QR vault.

OpenPGP.js, which docs/VAULT.md §10 names, is not run; sq does not seal a QR vault (below); rPGP judges the format only. §1.2's wider reading, which only Faraday's reader is held to, is not compared with a judge: any literal date, padding packets after the SEIPD packet and the literal data, and every length form RFC 9580 allows; of the chunk size octets only 0 (rPGP seals several chunks, Faraday opens them) and 10 are run.

Vectors The seven vaults of tools/vectors/vault/qr/ opened by sq, rPGP and the PyCA judge to the item each holds and by Faraday; the four refused messages refused by Faraday and by the PyCA judge; the PyCA judge refuses a vector with a byte changed in each field.

Random cases An item of every kind of §2.1 (12 and 24 words, a codex32 share, a passphrase, a note with markup, control characters and several scripts, the empty vault) sealed by Faraday and opened by sq, rPGP, the PyCA judge and Faraday, and sealed by rPGP and by the PyCA judge (memory 2^13 to 2^16 KiB) and opened by Faraday, each opened item read by tomllib; each memory step of §3 (2^16 to 2^20 KiB) sealed by Faraday at scale 1, each message equal byte for byte to the PyCA judge's seal of the same random bytes; items at the size limits (a note of 216 and 217 bytes, a passphrase of 193 and 194, a 24-word seed of the longest words); a passphrase in NFD or NFC either way; a wrong passphrase; a 15-word seed and a document of two keys sealed by rPGP, refused by Faraday; the messages sq writes, refused by Faraday and the PyCA judge; two items sealed by rPGP in chunks of 64 bytes (chunk size octet 0), opened by Faraday.

Differences QR vault: sq 1.3.1 writes a SKESK v4 and a SEIPD v1 for a password under either --profile, never the SKESK v6 and SEIPD v2 of RFC 9580, so sq cannot seal a QR vault; rPGP and the PyCA judge seal the other direction, and the area asserts that Faraday and the PyCA judge refuse what sq writes. The PyCA judge's framing is the area's own Python; OpenPGP.js is not run.

When it runs Before every release, with a new seed and about ten times the cases.

github.com/bitcoinpasada/faraday

Secret handling

none: no secret leaves faraday-keys

The tags are compared in constant time by the ocb3 crate; Argon2id, HKDF and AES state nothing more.

The Argon2 output, the wrapping key, the session key, the message key and the opened plaintext are Zeroizing values wiped on drop; the Argon2 memory is overwritten after the run.

Limits

A SKESK v4, a SEIPD v1, a public-key encrypted session key, a second SKESK, compressed data, a signature and trailing data but padding are named "An OpenPGP message Faraday does not open".

Argon2 memory 8 MiB to 1 GiB, passes 1 to 100 and lanes 1 to 64; outside them the message is refused right after the key packet, before the data packet is read or any memory is taken; a QR vault is written at 64 MiB to 1 GiB.

A wrong passphrase is told from a changed message: the session key's tag fails for the first, a data tag for the second.

The passphrase arrives in Unicode NFC; the caller puts it there.

Faraday's own calls

Only AES-256 with OCB and the Argon2 S2K are read: another cipher, AEAD mode or S2K is refused, as are armor and every packet but the three (F178, F190). Conservative, F190.

Libraries that are not established

The 3 libraries the actions use that are not established, each with the reason it is used and the decision that accepts it.

LibraryReasonDecision
lzma-rust2The Starter's xz decoder. No established pure-Rust streaming xz decoder exists, and the Starter's design (docs/STARTER.md) rules out the C library liblzma; what it writes is checked against the signed manifest's SHA-256 and size.F180
rqrrThe camera's QR decoder, vendored and patched against panics on hostile frames (third_party/rqrr/PATCHES.md): the only maintained pure-Rust QR decoder. What it reads is untrusted input that Faraday's parsers check. The same panic is reported upstream as rqrr's issue 54.F180
quick-xmlThe tokenizer under the XML of a KDBX vault file. It does no cryptography and has no outside review; its default features are off and it is already in the dependency graph. Which references are refused, the nesting cap and everything else the reader does are Faraday's own.F213
